messages.subject: Unusual behavior of plots when values of y are small
messages.subject_clean: Unusual behavior of plots when values of y are small
messages.body_plain:
The following code gives me a normal looking line plot:

    z <- data.frame(x = 1:5,  y = 1e-6 * c(1, 1.3, 1.5, -1.2, .8))
    ggplot(z, aes(x, y)) + geom_line()

However, if I let y be one order of magnitude smaller,

    z <- data.frame(x = 1:5,  y = 1e-7 * c(1, 1.3, 1.5, -1.2, .8))
   ggplot(z, aes(x, y)) + geom_line()

the plot is a straight line along y.  It seems that ggplot assumes
that all numbers below about 1e-6 are effectively the same.

I noticed this only in ggplot2 0.8.9, although I am not sure exactly
when this behavior started.  I definitely had normal looking line
plots in earlier versions of ggplot2.

Is this a bug or a feature, and is there a simple way to get normal
looking plots for small values of y without having to multiply all y
values by a constant?

----------------------------

Lester Wollman
Statistician
Symmetricom, Inc.

----------------------------------------------------------------------

Here my code

library(ggplot2)

# calculate lower and upper band
# for y
data$y.lower<-data$y.avg-data$y.lower
data$y.upper<-data$y.avg+data$y.upper
# for x
data$x.lower<-data$x.avg-data$x.lower
data$x.upper<-data$x.avg+data$x.upper

# calculate COD i.e. coefficient of divergence
cod<-round(sqrt(mean(((data$x.avg-data$y.avg)/(data$x.avg+data
$y.avg))^2)),3)

# chart
ggplot(data, aes(x.avg, y.avg, colour=labels))+

# vertical error bar
geom_errorbar(aes(ymin=y.lower, ymax=y.upper), size=0.1, width=0.1,
colour="red")+

# horizonal error bar
geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin=x.lower, xmax=x.upper), size=0.1, height=0.1,
colour="red")+

# diagonal line
geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1)+

# leading lines to point labels
geom_segment(aes(xend = x.label, yend = y.label), linetype = "dashed")
+

# points
geom_point(aes(colour=labels), size=2.5)+
#geom_point(size=2, colour="blue")+

# label position
geom_text(aes(label=labels, x = x.label, y = y.label), colour="black",
size=2.5, hjust=0, vjust=0)+

# y axis
scale_y_log10(name="y",
limits=c(1,1000),breaks=c(1,10,100,1000),formatter="scientific")+

#ylab("y")+

# x axis
scale_x_log10(name="x", limits=c(1,1000),
breaks=c(1,10,100,1000),formatter="scientific")+

#xlab("x")+

opts(title=cod, legend.position="right", legend.title="zzz")+

# background
theme_bw(base_size = 10)

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

beside that already present
How to control the key text of the legend? I want to change the text
“labels” in something else

How to control the type of legend ? e.g. a gradient between two
colours form green to red?

messages.subject: Re: GPU in ggplot
messages.subject_clean: GPU in ggplot
messages.body_plain:
This is ground up building differences.   The architecture is completely different.  You can take advantage of the gpu directly with packages like rgl, but that would require a rebuild of the architecture there.   The advantages of storing a plot as a specification that then can be output to may different channels (windows, x11, cairo, pdf, ps, etc.) far outweighs the slow plotting speed.

On another note, the R+GPU projects out there are mostly for doing general purpose computing on a GPU, but I don't think that is what was intended here.  I think it was something along the lines of directly plotting to the gpu to speed up rendering time, what graphics cards are intended for.  I'm going on a hunch here but I don't think that the actual rendering time is what is slowing things down.

-Andrew

messages.subject: scale_x_datetime: bug report and patch
messages.subject_clean: scale_x_datetime: bug report and patch
messages.body_plain:
Hoi,

I think there is a bug in the handling of the tz parameter of scale_x_datetime().  When major = 'day' this bug causes the major breaks not to be on day boundaries.

The cause of this bug is that not all methods that compute the labels and breaks take in account the specified timezone.

Below is an example that demonstrates this bug.

require(ggplot2)
start_date <- ISOdate( 2001, 12, 1, 0, 0, tz = "EST" )
timestamps <- start_date + seq( 0, 48*3600, by = 3600 )

testframe <- data.frame(
    tms  = timestamps,
    hour =  as.POSIXlt( timestamps )$hour
)

p <- ggplot( testframe, aes( x=tms, y=hour ) ) + geom_point() + geom_line()
plot1 <- p + scale_x_datetime(
           major = 'day',
           minor = '1 hour',
           tz="EST"
         )

This code create a dataframe with 48 timestamps.
Timestamps that start at 01 Dec 2001 00:00, incremented by 1 hour, and ends at 03 Dec 2001 00:00.
They are defined in the timezone EST, which is different from my timezone CET.

The dataframe also contains for each timestamp the hour component of each timestamp.  We plot the hour component as function of the timestamp with major breaks on the day boundary.

The resulting plot, plot1, is attached.

I have presumed the parameter tz to mean -- compute the labels and breaks in the specified timezone.
Since the specified timezone and the timezone of the dataset are equal I expected the following:
- the plot that starts at 01 Dec 2001 00:00
- the plot ends at 03 Dec 2001 00:00.
- The major breaks are at 01, 02, and 03 Dec (00:00 hours)
- A sawtooth wave that starts at 0 at the each major break.

The plot starts however well before 01 Dec and the sawtooth wave does not start at 0 at the major breaks.

Note that my own timezone is 'CET', and that the problem only occurs when the timezone used for the data is different from
my own timezone.  (If you happen to be living in a EST , change EST in the code to GMT to reproduce the bug.)

The following plot shows the reason (attached as plot2.png)

plot2 <- p + scale_x_datetime(
           major = 'day',
           minor = '1 hour',
           format="%d/%b %H:%M %Z",
           tz="EST"
        )

The major breaks are not on the day boundaries, but at 18:00 hours.

The problem is, I think, in scale-datetime.r in the methods input_breaks() and output_breaks().  After converting the
result of input_set() to time format with to_time().  The tz attribute is not set, and in further computations the tz of the system is used.

The following patch solves this problem.

https://github.com/gumpu/ggplot2/commit/ee1487df47d89d8c69c88ff73d2a2fd512de6c50

The attached plot plot1_fixed.png shows the result of the patch.

Dennis

I was able to reproduce the same bug you have by setting my timezone
to 'EST'.

Was able to fix the problem by setting the tz parameter  for scale_x_datetime() to this same timezone,  ie:

scale_x_datetime(limits = c(as.POSIXct("2010-11-06"),

                as.POSIXct("2010-11-10")), minor="1 day", tz=Sys.timezone())

Maybe this works for you too.

Have fun,
Frans.

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I was able to reproduce this bug under Linux by running:

   TZ='America/New_York'; export TZ

before running R.

Under Linux the fix:

   scale_x_datetime(limits = c(as.POSIXct("2010-11-06"),
                as.POSIXct("2010-11-10")), minor="1 day", tz=Sys.timezone())

does not work,  but

  scale_x_datetime(limits = c(as.POSIXct("2010-11-06"),

                as.POSIXct("2010-11-10")), minor="1 day", tz='EST')
does.

This bug might be triggered by the fact that in the EST timezone day light savings
ended on 07 Nov in 2010.
Which is right in the given data series,  and it also happens to be the day that is repeated.

Have fun,
Frans.

On 2 February 2011 00:21, Dennis Murphy <djm...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi:
>
> I think this is related to the repeated date issue reported by Sarah McKinnon in another thread. When I looked at her data briefly, I extracted the date part and converted it with as.Date(). Comparing the new dates with the old (which contained H:M:S + ...) information, I noticed there was a 7-hour offset between the correct day in her original data and the day reported with the created variable (the number of hours may be due to a time zone difference - mine is PST [US]).
>
> HTH,
> Dennis
>
> On Tue, Feb 1, 2011 at 2:00 PM, Frans Slothouber <frans.sl...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hoi,
> >
> > I think there is a bug in the handling of the tz parameter of scale_x_datetime().  When major = 'day' this bug causes the major breaks not to be on day boundaries.
> >
> > The cause of this bug is that not all methods that compute the labels and breaks take in account the specified timezone.
> >
> > Below is an example that demonstrates this bug.
> >
> > require(ggplot2)
> > start_date <- ISOdate( 2001, 12, 1, 0, 0, tz = "EST" )
> > timestamps <- start_date + seq( 0, 48*3600, by = 3600 )
> >
> > testframe <- data.frame(
> >     tms  = timestamps,
> >     hour =  as.POSIXlt( timestamps )$hour
> > )
> >
> > p <- ggplot( testframe, aes( x=tms, y=hour ) ) + geom_point() + geom_line()
> > plot1 <- p + scale_x_datetime(
> >            major = 'day',
> >            minor = '1 hour',
> >            tz="EST"
> >          )
> >
> > This code create a dataframe with 48 timestamps.
> > Timestamps that start at 01 Dec 2001 00:00, incremented by 1 hour, and ends at 03 Dec 2001 00:00.
> > They are defined in the timezone EST, which is different from my timezone CET.
> >
> > The dataframe also contains for each timestamp the hour component of each timestamp.  We plot the hour component as function of the timestamp with major breaks on the day boundary.
> >
> > The resulting plot, plot1, is attached.
> >
> >
> > I have presumed the parameter tz to mean -- compute the labels and breaks in the specified timezone.
> > Since the specified timezone and the timezone of the dataset are equal I expected the following:
> > - the plot that starts at 01 Dec 2001 00:00
> > - the plot ends at 03 Dec 2001 00:00.
> > - The major breaks are at 01, 02, and 03 Dec (00:00 hours)
> > - A sawtooth wave that starts at 0 at the each major break.
> >
> > The plot starts however well before 01 Dec and the sawtooth wave does not start at 0 at the major breaks.
> >
> > Note that my own timezone is 'CET', and that the problem only occurs when the timezone used for the data is different from
> > my own timezone.  (If you happen to be living in a EST , change EST in the code to GMT to reproduce the bug.)
> >
> >
> > The following plot shows the reason (attached as plot2.png)
> >
> > plot2 <- p + scale_x_datetime(
> >            major = 'day',
> >            minor = '1 hour',
> >            format="%d/%b %H:%M %Z",
> >            tz="EST"
> >         )
> >
> > The major breaks are not on the day boundaries, but at 18:00 hours.
> >
> > The problem is, I think, in scale-datetime.r in the methods input_breaks() and output_breaks().  After converting the
> > result of input_set() to time format with to_time().  The tz attribute is not set, and in further computations the tz of the system is used.
> >
> >
> > The following patch solves this problem.
> >
> > https://github.com/gumpu/ggplot2/commit/ee1487df47d89d8c69c88ff73d2a2fd512de6c50
> >
> > The attached plot plot1_fixed.png shows the result of the patch.

> > Platform: x86_64-pc-linux-gnu (64-bit)

messages.subject: Re: GPU in ggplot
messages.subject_clean: GPU in ggplot
messages.body_plain:
I think the GPU part of this question has been answered in multiple ways, however, the main stumbling block in ggplot speed is that it is all of the R code in the package.   If only we had a decent R JIT compiler.

The other alternative for speed would be to rewrite ggplot in a low-level language.   I'm a huge fan of ggplot and would love to see its facilities even outside of R where it could be called programmatically (without R evaluation).

Could only wish to roll back history and build the language on top of one of the successful JIT VMs.     R's lazy expression resolution and evaluation would make this quite challenging, but doable.   Probably the most challenging scripting language to compile.

messages.subject: Re: GPU in ggplot
messages.subject_clean: GPU in ggplot
messages.body_plain:
> I think the GPU part of this question has been answered in multiple ways, however, the main stumbling block in ggplot speed is that it is all of the R code in the package.   If only we had a decent R JIT compiler.
>
> The other alternative for speed would be to rewrite ggplot in a low-level language.   I'm a huge fan of ggplot and would love to see its facilities even outside of R where it could be called programmatically (without R evaluation).

I honestly don't think that ggplot2 is slow because of R - it's slow
because at the time I wrote it, I didn't know how to write efficient
code in R.  If I knew then what I know now, it would be much much
faster.

I am slowly working towards a faster version of ggplot2.  However,
progress is slow, because it requires a lot of refactoring and
cleaning up of the basics - I can't make it fast until I can ensure it
continues to work, and works in a way that I actually understand.  The
other problem is that this is the sort of work that I have to do in my
spare time - it's pure software development, not research.

I would love to have an assistant, but it really would require a
substantial time investment, and I don't currently have access to the
financial resources to fund someone long term.  A summer is easy to
find money for - two years is not.

> Could only wish to roll back history and build the language on top of one of the successful JIT VMs.     R's lazy expression resolution and evaluation would make this quite challenging, but doable.   Probably the most challenging scripting language to compile.

There's a group in the CS department at Stanford working on an R
implementation built on top of Lua - the Lua JIT is extremely fast,
and has much better support for dynamic language features than the
JVM.

Hadley

messages.subject: Re: GPU in ggplot
messages.subject_clean: GPU in ggplot
messages.body_plain:
Am 02.02.2011 um 16:23 schrieb Hadley Wickham:
>> The other alternative for speed would be to rewrite ggplot in a low-level language.   I'm a huge fan of ggplot and would love to see its facilities even outside of R where it could be called programmatically (without R evaluation).
>
> I honestly don't think that ggplot2 is slow because of R - it's slow
> because at the time I wrote it, I didn't know how to write efficient
> code in R.  If I knew then what I know now, it would be much much
> faster.

I have to underline what Hadley said. Porting loops from R code to some other language or hoping for a JIT doesn't give much speedup. In order to exploit the underlying structure of computations, they have to be expressed in higher level terms -- not lower-level languages. For example, when you replace loops over vectors by proper vector operations, the R system will perform them with nicely optimized, built-in machine code already.
Thus, most of the expensive operations could be done quickly if the built-in operations were used.

The research group I am working in, is currently looking into implementing distributed data frames in C++. The aim is to make programming parallel computations on data frames much easier (even on distributed memory systems). I personally think that it is possible to have something like google's MapReduce framework or rply based on such distributed data frames. In this regard I guess that no JIT will have the reasoning power to transform a bunch of loops into a high-level description exploitable by such a system.

> I am slowly working towards a faster version of ggplot2.

Would be interesting to see, which kind of expensive/complex operations are used typically.

> spare time - it's pure software development, not research.

It is the same here: making such frameworks usable inside R would most probably be pure marketing.

Randolf Rotta

--
PhD student / research assistant
Computer Science Department
Brandenburg University of Technology, Cottbus, Germay

messages.body_plain:
On Feb 2, 2011, at 12:43 PM, Randolf Rotta wrote:

>
> Am 02.02.2011 um 16:23 schrieb Hadley Wickham:
>>> The other alternative for speed would be to rewrite ggplot in a low-level language.   I'm a huge fan of ggplot and would love to see its facilities even outside of R where it could be called programmatically (without R evaluation).
>>
>> I honestly don't think that ggplot2 is slow because of R - it's slow
>> because at the time I wrote it, I didn't know how to write efficient
>> code in R.  If I knew then what I know now, it would be much much
>> faster.
>
> I have to underline what Hadley said. Porting loops from R code to some other language or hoping for a JIT doesn't give much speedup. In order to exploit the underlying structure of computations, they have to be expressed in higher level terms -- not lower-level languages. For example, when you replace loops over vectors by proper vector operations, the R system will perform them with nicely optimized, built-in machine code already.
> Thus, most of the expensive operations could be done quickly if the built-in operations were used.
>

(I'm not holding my breath on R JIT ;)   I've looked at LuaJIT and am quite impressed with its performance.   Hopefully the Stanford R -> luaVM work makes it out of research.

As for speeding up R code in general you can certainly go a long way with the use of vector primitives and avoiding an imperative style.   However, I find that there are dramatic slowdowns as soon as your vector function, say, apply() needs to call a script based function.   Evaluation of R code proper is much slower than any modern scripting language I've used.

For data-parallel problems one can make use of snow or other distribution approaches, however, in some cases (like mine), I have to do stateful computations, where the result of one computation requires that of the preceding.   Hence R evaluation speed presents difficulties for me.

I use R as opposed to Clojure or any number of other functional languages out there just because it has such a large package base and core statistics functionality.   Moving a small fraction of this to another language environment is a huge endeavor.

Jonathan Shore
--
Systematic Trading Group

The best I can do is provide you with the syntax that creates the data frame that I'm plotting and a bit of dummy data:

df.tmp <- data.frame(rep(letters[1:10],100), rep(1:4,250))
colnames(df.tmp) <- c("value","variable")
df.tmp <- cast(df.tmp, variable + value ~ ., length, fill=c(0), add.missing=T)
colnames(df.tmp)[3] <- c("frequ")

df.tmp <- ddply(df.tmp,"variable", function(x) {
        x <- x[order(x$value),]
        x$cfreq <- cumsum(x$frequ)/sum(x$frequ)
        x$pos <- (c(0,x$cfreq[-nrow(x)])+x$cfreq)/2
        x$freq <- (x$frequ)/sum(x$frequ)
        x
    })

df.tmp1 <- data.frame(df.tmp, year=2010)
df.tmp2 <- data.frame(df.tmp, year=2011)

df.tmp <- rbind(df.tmp1, df.tmp2)

panel.1 <- list(opts(panel.background=theme_blank(), panel.grid.minor=theme_blank(), panel.grid.major=theme_blank(), axis.text.x=theme_blank(), legend.position="right", axis.ticks=theme_blank()))

plot.tmp <- ggplot(df.tmp, aes(year,frequ, fill=value)) + geom_bar(stat="identity", position="fill") + scale_y_continuous("", formatter="percent") + geom_bar(position="dodge")  + labs(x="",y="", fill="") + panel.1 + opts(title="Work Damnit!") + facet_grid(. ~ variable)

messages.body_plain:
I had the same problem and found a work around:
Add a phantom point outside the plotting range with the size that you
want in the legend:

Say you have:
df=data.frame(x=c(0,1),y=c(2,0),C=c('blue','red'))
Graph=ggplot(data=df,mapping=aes(x=x,y=y,color=C),size=0.1)+geom_point()

Add a phantom point outside the plotting range - which you need to fix
explicity (pain/gain)
Graph=Graph+
      geom_point(data=data.frame(x=3,y=1,C='red'),size=3)+
      coord_cartesian(xlim=c(-.1,1.1))+

messages.subject: Creating multiple sets of labels for the x and y axes
messages.subject_clean: Creating multiple sets of labels for the x and y axes
messages.body_plain:
I wanted to resurrect this thread <https://groups.google.com/d/topic/ggplot2/YVVEgqQGRXI/discussion> in light of some design considerations I'm going through.

Regarding multiple axes, Hadley wrote last year:
> Laying the ground work for a secondary transformed axis is on my to do list for this summer.
I was wondering whether it's possible to have multiple sets of labels for the same breaks. In Andrie's code, he solves the problem of having both fahrenheit and celsius values by concatenating them. He passes farhenheit-celsius pairs as entries to the "labels" argument of scale_x_continuous:

## Andrie's Code
degC <- seq(0,100,10)
degCandF <- paste(degC,"C / ",degC * 9 / 5 + 32,"F",sep="")
d <- data.frame(tempcelcius=round(rnorm(25,15, 10), 1),attendence=rnorm(25,500, 100))
p <- qplot(x=tempcelcius,y=attendence,data=d)
p <- p + scale_x_continuous("Temperature (Celsius/Fahrenheit)",breaks=degC,labels=degCandF)
print(p)

In the code below, I create a situation—albeit a slightly nonsense one—where for international audiences it might be sensible to have converted values appear.

## My Code
set.seed(seed = 1001)
Dollars      <- seq(20000, 40000, 2000)
DollarLabels <- paste("$", Dollars)

Pounds       <- seq(6, 11, 1)
PoundLabels  <- paste(Pounds, "lbs.")

d <- data.frame(AnnualIncome = rnorm(n = 25, mean = 30000, sd = 2500), BirthWeight = rnorm(n = 25, mean = 8, sd = 1))
p <- qplot(x = AnnualIncome, y = BirthWeight, data = d)
p <- p + scale_x_continuous("Annual Income", breaks = Dollars, labels = DollarLabels)
p <- p + scale_y_continuous("Birth Weight", breaks = Pounds, labels = PoundLabels)
print(p)

For example, the graph might be useful to international audiences if they could view it in terms of other currencies and international standard weights. In the image I've created (attached), I made up the currency and weight conversions for ease of mock-up. The key feature, though, is to assume that the major gridlines represent the same real unit of weight/money, and all I'm doing is supplying labels that respectively represent that weight/amount through a localised conversion. I don't want new breaks, just the ability to supply multiple sets of converted labels—in different positions—for the same underlying break numbers.

Does that make sense? If so, my colleague and I were wondering whether the solution might lie in either a crafty geom_text() call, or creating a modified geom based off of geom_text() to handle placing the labels. (We're not sure how we'd implement it exactly, yet.)

Alternatively, if you think there are better ways to display converted information for the same breaks, I'd love to hear your suggestions. It just seemed like having converted values on another axis was sensible. But I welcome your feedback and input!

- Brian

messages.subject_clean: help with boxplot outliers/ggplot magic
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben,

A few points:

 * you're better off using outlier.colour = NULL, then checking with
is.null instead of missing - this makes it easier to see what's going
on regardless of how draw is called

 * using with makes it confusing to understand where variables are
being pulled from - the next version of ggplot will make much less use
of with

So all in all, I'd probably do something like this:

    if (!is.null(data$outliers) && length(data$outliers[[1]] >= 1)) {
      outlier_data <- data.frame(
        y = data$outliers[[1]],
        x = data$x[1],
        colour = outlier.colour %||% data$colour[1],
        shape =  outlier.shape %||% data$shape[1],
        size =  outlier.size %||% data$size[1],
        fill = NA,
        alpha = 1,
        stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
      outliers_grob <- GeomPoint$draw(outlier_data, ...)
    } else {
      outliers_grob <- NULL
    }

But don't have time to try it out right now.

Hadley

messages.body_plain:
Hadley,

In a conversation about boxplots yesterday, I realized something about the implementation in ggplot2. The median line is the same width as all of the other lines - it should be thicker. The primary comparison that people need to make between distributions is based on the medians of the groups, then the spread which is the box. And outliers are somewhat separate piece of information - you already have the ability to increase the focus on outliers if desired.

Can you increase the line width for the median and make this the default? Or at least allow the thickness of this line to be changed.

cheers,
Di
---------------------------
Dianne Cook
dic...@iastate.edu

p = p + scale_x_date(lim = c(as.Date("2011-01-18"), as.Date("2011-02-25")))

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

A lot of things occur here.

first,

my_theme <- theme_update(panel.background = theme_blank(), axis.text.x
= theme_text(colour = "black"), axis.text.y = theme_text(colour =
"black"), axis.title.x = theme_text(colour = "black", face = "bold"),
axis.title.y = theme_text(colour = "black", face = "bold", angle =
90), panel.grid.minor = theme_blank(),
 panel.grid.major = theme_blank(), panel.background = theme_blank(),
axis.line = theme_segment())

theme_set() and theme_update() modify the current theme and returns
*old* current theme.
so my_theme refers the old theme, and the current theme is the theme
that you gave.

then,

last_plot() + theme_set(my_theme)

the theme_set returns the old theme (i.e., one you gave), and set the
my_theme (i.e., default theme) as the current theme.
but this call have theme, the current theme is ignored and the theme
that theme_set() returned is used.

then, next call

last_plot() + theme_set(my_theme)

here, the current theme before the call is my_theme (i.e., default theme),
so theme_set returns the default theme.

finally, if you set the theme permanently in your session, then simply,

theme_update(panel.background = theme_blank(), axis.text.x
= theme_text(colour = "black"), axis.text.y = theme_text(colour =
"black"), axis.title.x = theme_text(colour = "black", face = "bold"),
axis.title.y = theme_text(colour = "black", face = "bold", angle =
90), panel.grid.minor = theme_blank(),
 panel.grid.major = theme_blank(), panel.background = theme_blank(),
axis.line = theme_segment())

qplot(1:2)
qplot(1:2, 3:4)

this is okey.

maybe my english is too poor to explain these things...
but hope this helps.

--

The University of  Tokyo, Japan.

messages.subject: Re: masked object
messages.subject_clean: masked object
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

On Sat, Feb 5, 2011 at 9:28 PM, ericstrom <eric.th...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Getting the following message when I load ggplot2 :
>
> library(ggplot2)
> Loading required package: reshape
> Loading required package: plyr
>
> Attaching package: 'reshape'
>
> The following object(s) are masked from 'package:plyr':
>
>    round_any
>
> Loading required package: grid
> Loading required package: proto
>
> What causes the object to be masked and is this a problem? Note that
> loaded ggplot as soon as I opened my R session.

What causes the masking is two or more loaded packages with the same function name. The convention in R is that the version from the most recently loaded package will be used by default. It's generally not a problem unless the function you *really* want is the one that is masked. This is not a major problem, however, because one can specify a package-function combination with a double colon in between. Here's a small example:

> x <- rnorm(5)
> plyr::round_any(x, 2)
[1]  0  0 -2  0  2
> reshape::round_any(x, 2)
[1]  0  0 -2  0  2

Preceding a function name by its package with a :: separator selects the version of the function in question in the package specified. In this case, the function round_any() is the same in both packages, as verified by checking the code in each version - the only difference between them is their namespace.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.body_plain:
Chase, from SO, was kind enough to provide this solution (http://stackoverflow.com/questions/4917570/r-creating-custom-shapes-with-ggplot):

It seems like you could use a combination of geom_path() and geom_segment() since you either know or can reasonably guesstimate the coordinate locations for each major point on your graph/chart/thingamajigger up there. Maybe something like this would work? The data.frame that was constructed contains the outline of the shape above (I opted for the rectangle at the top...I'm sure you could find an easy way to generate the points to approximate a circle if you really wanted. Then use geom_segment() to divvy up that large shape as you need.
df <- data.frame(
    x = c(-8,-4,4,8,-8, -8, -8, 8, 8, -8)
    , y = c(0,18,18,0,0, 18, 22, 22, 18, 18)
    , group = c(rep(1,5), rep(2,5)))

qplot(x,y, data = df, geom = "path", group = group)+
    geom_segment(aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = 0, yend = 12 )) +
    geom_segment(aes(x = -6.75, y = 6, xend = 6.75, yend = 6)) +
    geom_segment(aes(x = -5.25, y = 12, xend = 5.25, yend = 12)) +
    geom_segment(aes(x = -2, y = 12, xend = -2, yend = 18)) +
    geom_segment(aes(x = 2, y = 12, xend = 2, yend = 18)) +
    geom_text(aes(x = -5, y = 2.5), label = "hi world")

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Why don't you use grid graphics directly?

library(gridExtra)

grid.newpage()
grid.ellipse(0.5, 0.8, ar=2.5, size=0.3, angle=pi,
             default.units="npc", size.units="npc", gp=gpar(fill=rgb(0, 113, 193, max=256)))

x <- c(0.5, 0.5, 0.45, 0.4, 0.5)
y <- c(0.65, 0.75, 0.75, 0.65, 0.65)

grid.polygon(x, y, gp=gpar(fill=rgb(163, 163, 223, max=256)))
grid.polygon(1-x, y, gp=gpar(fill=rgb(163, 163, 223, max=256)))

x2 <- c(0.4, 0.35, 0.5, 0.5, 0.4)
y2 <- c(0.65, 0.55, 0.55, 0.65, 0.65)

grid.polygon(x2, y2, gp=gpar(fill=rgb(209, 210, 240, max=256)))
grid.polygon(1-x2, y2, gp=gpar(fill=rgb(209, 210, 240, max=256)))

x3 <- c(0.35, 0.3, 0.5, 0.5, 0.35)
y3 <- c(0.55, 0.45, 0.45, 0.55, 0.55)

grid.polygon(x3, y3, gp=gpar(fill=rgb(217, 217, 217, max=256)))
grid.polygon(1-x3, y3, gp=gpar(fill=rgb(217, 217, 217, max=256)))

x4 <- c(0.5, 0.47)
y4 <- c(0.8, 0.7)
labels <- c("ellipse", "top")

grid.text(labels, x4,y4)

HTH,

baptiste

messages.subject_clean: matching geom_point size to the geom_tile size
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm trying to combine geom_tile with geom_point to show three aspects of
a comparison between days:  ( count, mean, and max ).

The following code creates and example of this.

require(ggplot2)

d1 <- as.Date("2009-10-01")
d2 <- as.Date("2009-10-15")
xd  <- rep( seq(d1,d2,by="day"), each=15 )
yd  <- rep( seq(d1,d2,by="day"), 15 )

mm <- data.frame( xd=xd, yd=yd )
mm$mean  <- runif( nrow(mm), min=1, max=2 )
mm$max   <- runif( nrow(mm), min=2, max=3 )
mm$count <- floor( runif( nrow(mm), min=-24, max=24 ) )

p <- ggplot( mm, aes( x=xd, y=yd ) ) +
     geom_tile( aes(fill=count ), colour="black", space="Lab" ) +
     geom_point( aes( size=max ), alpha=0.4 ) +
     geom_point( aes( size=mean ), colour="white" ) +
     scale_fill_gradient2( limits=c( -24, 24 ),
        name="high/low\ncount",
         low="darkgreen",
         mid="yellow",
        high="darkred") +
     scale_size( name="Maximum\nand mean\ndifference\nin hourly\nmean" )

ggsave( plot=p, "example.png", width=5, height=5 )

My problem is that this works well if I compare a set of 15 days,
that is the size of the points and the size of the tiles match.
However if my data set contains only a few days, the points look way too small,
and when I have many days, the points look too big compared to the tiles.

Is there a way to match the point size to the tile size?

I've attached an example of a the plot I like (example) and the one
with points that are too small (example1.png)

Have fun,
Frans.

James

One workaround is to add a fairly arbitratry, large positive number to
the x-values.  For example, use 180 or 360.

library(ggplot2)

require(maps)
world <- data.frame(map("world", plot=FALSE)[c("x","y")])

world$x <- world$x + 360

ggplot( world, aes(x=x,y=y)) + geom_path( ) + coord_map()

This will result in a map without horizontal lines, *but* will clearly
only be useful if it is not important to have the longitude labelled.

Andrie

messages.subject: Re: matching geom_point size to the geom_tile size
messages.subject_clean: matching geom_point size to the geom_tile size
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

The 'obvious' solution would be to create a multiplier for the point sizes that would be proportional to the area of a tile, but I believe you run into certain limitations inside ggplot2 per se since the sizes rendered seem to be relative to the maximum size rather than the size itself. Compare the following:

dd <- data.frame(x = 1:5, y = 1:5, sz = (1:5)^2)
ggplot(dd, aes(x, y)) + geom_point(aes(size = sz))
# windows()      # start up new graphics device of choice

# Compare the max and min sizes of the two graphs
dev.off(dev.cur())    # Turn off most recently created device

The physical size of the largest point is the same in the two plots, but the ratio of (max/min)^2 seems to be maintained.

For five-day data (d2 <- as.Date('2009-10-05')), I tried computing a size multiplier parameter of

sz <- 225/(length(unique(xd))^2)

which one would hope would increase the physical point size by a factor of 9 relative to the 15-day plot, but it doesn't. I squared the result and tried again - the result was a not too dissimilar plot. The primary observation is that the maximum physical point size is the same in both plots. It's possible that it is hard-coded in ggplot2, which is suggested by the initial tests above. One possible way out may be to hack the code with the grid package, or wait for one of the experts to do it for you :) I haven't ventured into the grid jungle yet...

I tried it again for 20 days and 30 days, and although the points took up a larger proportion of the area than the 15 day plot, they looked OK to me, which suggests that, for the 'many-day' plots, some ratio of point size relative to tile size seems to work. [The above 'formula' for sz is a pure hack for testing the concept - it's not meant to be taken seriously.] As for the 'few day' plots, you have an absolute size problem to deal with, I believe, as noted above.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

This works:

library(lattice)
library(latticeExtra)   # where the data frame resides
data(gvhd10)

ph <- ggplot(gvhd10, aes(x = log(FSC.H)))
ph + geom_ribbon(aes(ymax = ..density.., ymin = -..density..),

                          stat = "density") +

facet_grid(Days ~ ., as.table = FALSE,  scales = "free_y") +
xlab("log(Forward Scatter)")

You don't want Days as either an x or y aesthetic because you intend to use it as the grouping variable. The log(FSC.H) is the 'x' variable because it plays a role similar to that in geom_density() or geom_histogram() - it provides the domain for the estimated density to be computed.  ..density.. is the y-variable. The appearance has to do with the combination of the way that the plot is generated and the formula used for facet_grid().  [Think of a violin as a density plot reflected around its x-axis; this is why log(FSC.H) is the x variable.] To reproduce this structure by groups, Days has to be the 'y' variable in the facet_grid() formula so that each panel has ..density.. as its 'y'.

To do this in the other direction, we have to create a single violin plot as a separate object, using coord_flip() to switch the x and y axis,. We can then partition it by Days using facet_grid() again, except with Days on the RHS (x) this time. A couple of extra code chunks are added/modified to improve its appearance.

# Generate a violin plot and flip the x and y axes
pj <- ggplot(gvhd10, aes(x = log(FSC.H))) +

      geom_ribbon(aes(ymax = ..density.., ymin = -..density..),

                          stat = "density") + coord_flip() +
      opts(axis.text.x = theme_text(angle = 90, hjust = 0.5)) +
      ylab("log(Forward Scatter)")
# Plot by groups with facet_grid()
pj + facet_grid(. ~ Days, scales = 'free_x' )

Hopefully, you can see the coordination that has to exist between the 'base' violin plot and facet_grid().

HTH,
Dennis

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

On Wed, Feb 9, 2011 at 12:00 PM, <Adam_L...@keybank.com> wrote:
>
> What does the "as.table" argument do basically, within the facet_grid?
>
> Other than affecting the order in which the group variables appear, I'm having trouble seeing what difference it makes. Is that it's only purpose?

Yes. The idea was initially in lattice, which by default starts panels in the lower left corner, works to the right and then ascends in succeeding rows. After many complaints by people who wanted the panels ordered in the opposite direction,  Deepayan came up with the as.table argument in xyplot.  The use in ggplot2 emulates that idea. It tends to have more impact in 2D arrays of plots than in 1D, which may account for your perception of its usefulness :)

Dennis

> ph + geom_ribbon(aes(ymax = ..density.., ymin = -..density..),
>                           stat = "density") +
> facet_grid(Days ~ ., as.table = FALSE,  scales = "free_y") +
> xlab("log(Forward Scatter)")
>
> You don't want Days as either an x or y aesthetic because you intend to use it as the grouping variable. The log(FSC.H) is the 'x' variable because it plays a role similar to that in geom_density() or geom_histogram() - it provides the domain for the estimated density to be computed.  ..density.. is the y-variable. The appearance has to do with the combination of the way that the plot is generated and the formula used for facet_grid().  [Think of a violin as a density plot reflected around its x-axis; this is why log(FSC.H) is the x variable.] To reproduce this structure by groups, Days has to be the 'y' variable in the facet_grid() formula so that each panel has ..density.. as its 'y'.
>
> To do this in the other direction, we have to create a single violin plot as a separate object, using coord_flip() to switch the x and y axis,. We can then partition it by Days using facet_grid() again, except with Days on the RHS (x) this time. A couple of extra code chunks are added/modified to improve its appearance.

> # Generate a violin plot and flip the x and y axes
> pj <- ggplot(gvhd10, aes(x = log(FSC.H))) +
>       geom_ribbon(aes(ymax = ..density.., ymin = -..density..),
>                           stat = "density") + coord_flip() +
>       opts(axis.text.x = theme_text(angle = 90, hjust = 0.5)) +
>       ylab("log(Forward Scatter)")
> # Plot by groups with facet_grid()
> pj + facet_grid(. ~ Days, scales = 'free_x' )
>
> Hopefully, you can see the coordination that has to exist between the 'base' violin plot and facet_grid().

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

It's a lot easier to get useful help if you supply a small example, with data and code, that illustrates the problem you're having. For one thing, since no one has access to your data, it's impossible to run your code to see what it produces - one can only guess and hope that our imagination matches your reality. That's error prone.

Based on your graph outline below, perhaps you're looking for something like the following:

# Create a toy data set with three variables
df <- data.frame(grp = rep(c('A', 'B'), each = 20),
                   Y1 = rnorm(40),
                   Y2 = rnorm(40, mean = 3, sd = 2))

# To get 'side-by side' boxplots of the two variables by groups, the first step
# is to 'stack' the data by using the melt() function in the reshape package - it
# loads with ggplot2. The result is a data frame with a grp column (id variable),
# a factor named variable that identifies the variable name, and a variable named
# value that contains the values of the two variables Y1 and Y2 (which are assumed to
# be comparable in the graph below). This can be used to advantage in the ggplot() call.
dfm <- melt(df, id = 'grp')

# Note how the created factor 'variable' is used as an aesthetic:
ggplot(dfm, aes(x = grp, y = value)) +
     geom_boxplot(aes(fill = variable))

In this example, the fill aesthetic allows the boxplots to be 'dodged' next to one another within the same grp, with a legend that identifies the variables associated with each fill color.

If the response variables are different from each other, an alternative is to produce a faceted plot, with the variables generating individual facets:

ggplot(dfm, aes(x = grp, y = value)) + labs(fill = 'Group', x = 'Group', y = 'Response') +
     geom_boxplot(aes(fill = grp)) + facet_wrap( ~ variable, scales = 'free_y')

In this plot, the 'free_y' scale allows for different y-scales in each panel; without it, both facets have the same x- and y-scales. The labs() statement provides labels for the legend title (fill) as well as for the x and y axis; it is convenient and worth remembering, since AFAIR it wasn't mentioned in Hadley's book.

Hope this is what you were after,
Dennis

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

several weeks ago I wrote a geom-circle function for my own purpose,
but probably it is relevant to what you want.
here is an example code. maybe you can find your solution.

GeomCircle <- proto(Geom, {

  default_stat <- function(.) StatIdentity
  default_pos <- function(.) PositionIdentity
  default_aes <- function(.) aes(colour=NA, fill="grey20", radius=0.5,
linetype=1, alpha = 1)

  required_aes <- c("x", "y")

  draw <- draw_groups <- function(., data, scales, coordinates, ...) {
    data <- remove_missing(data, na.rm,
      c("x", "y", "radius"), name = "geom_circle")
    if (empty(data)) return(zeroGrob())
    with(coordinates$transform(data, scales),
      ggname(.$my_name(), circleGrob(x, y, r = radius, default.unit = "native",
      gp=gpar(col=alpha(colour, alpha), fill = alpha(fill, alpha))))
    )
  }
  objname <- "circle"
  guide_geom <- function(.) "polygon"

})
geom_circle <- GeomCircle$build_accessor()

d1 <- as.Date("2009-10-01")
d2 <- as.Date("2009-10-15")
xd  <- rep( seq(d1,d2,by="day"), each=15 )
yd  <- rep( seq(d1,d2,by="day"), 15 )

mm <- data.frame( xd=xd, yd=yd )
mm$mean  <- runif( nrow(mm), min=1, max=2 )
mm$max   <- runif( nrow(mm), min=2, max=3 )
mm$count <- floor( runif( nrow(mm), min=-24, max=24 ) )

mm <- transform(mm, smean = mean/base::max(max), smax = max/base::max(max))

radius <- 1/2/max(length(unique(mm$xd)), length(unique(mm$yd)))

p <- ggplot( mm, aes( x=xd, y=yd ) ) +

geom_tile( aes(fill=count), colour="black", space="Lab" ) +
geom_circle(aes(radius=radius*smax), alpha=0.4) +
geom_circle(aes(radius=radius*smean), fill="white", colour="white") +

scale_fill_gradient2( limits=c( -24, 24 ),
 name="high/low\ncount",
 low="darkgreen",
 mid="yellow",
 high="darkred") +
 scale_size( name="Maximum\nand mean\ndifference\nin hourly\nmean" )

mm2 <- subset(mm, xd < 14523 & yd < 14522)

radius <- 1/2/max(length(unique(mm2$xd)), length(unique(mm2$yd)))

p <- ggplot( mm2, aes( x=xd, y=yd ) ) +
geom_tile( aes(fill=count), colour="black", space="Lab" ) +
geom_circle(aes(radius=radius*smax), alpha=0.4) +
geom_circle(aes(radius=radius*smean), fill="white", colour="white") +

scale_fill_gradient2( limits=c( -24, 24 ),
 name="high/low\ncount",
 low="darkgreen",
 mid="yellow",
 high="darkred") +
 scale_size( name="Maximum\nand mean\ndifference\nin hourly\nmean" )

messages.subject: normal quantile plot with straight line
messages.subject_clean: normal quantile plot with straight line
messages.body_plain:
Consider the following very common task. Given a quantitative variable, we want to make a normal quantile plot. And we want to run a straight line through the plot. This is easily done in traditional graphics. For instance:

set.seed(7)
DUT<- data.frame( stuff=round(rnorm(7), 2))

qqnorm(DUT$stuff)
qqline(DUT$stuff)

Am I correct in believing that there is no elegant way to perform this task in ggplot2, i.e., no way that exploits the grammar of graphics and the statistical transformation functions as implemented in ggplot2?

Here's how to make the normal quantile plot in ggplot2 without the straight line:

require(ggplot2)
ggplot(data=DUT, mapping=aes( sample=stuff))  + stat_qq(shape=1)

Here is a workaround for putting the line on the plot in ggplot2. For the statistical transformation, we fall back on traditional graphics:

ggplot(data=as.data.frame( qqnorm(DUT$stuff, plot=FALSE)), aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_point(shape=1) + geom_smooth(method="lm", se=FALSE) + scale_x_continuous(name="Theoretical quantiles") + scale_y_continuous(name="Sample quantiles")

In this case, the only reason to use ggplot2 seems to be if we have mastered the options in that package and want a consistent color scheme, etc.

If we wish to avoid using a traditional graphics function, the following works.

DUT$Sample<-rev(DUT$stuff)
DUT$Theoretical<- qnorm(ppoints(nrow(DUT)))[order(DUT$Sample)]
ggplot(  data=DUT, mapping=aes(x=Theoretical, y=Sample) ) + geom_point(shape=1) + geom_smooth(method="lm", se=FALSE)

but again it makes no use of the concept of statistical transformations as implemented in ggplot2.

In the normal quantile plot, the statistical transformation transforms the sample into two vectors: the theoretical and sample quantiles. The qqnorm() function returns them as x and y, and we exploited them above.

The documentation of stat_qq at http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/stat_qq.html says that this function produces two new variables, "..sample.." and "..theoretical..", which are probably identical to the y and x vectors returned by qqnorm(). But how does one obtain these variables?

A search using str() can be conducted as follows:

what<-stat_qq(data=DUT, mapping=aes(sample=stuff))
str(what)
whatAgain<-ggplot() + what
str(whatAgain)

but from the difficulty finding ..theoretical.. and ..sample.. this way, I conclude that we are not intended to find or access these vectors.

Thanks for any insights.

Jacob A. Wegelin
Assistant Professor
Department of Biostatistics
Virginia Commonwealth University

P. O. Box 980032
Richmond VA 23298-0032
U.S.A.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Ista,

Thank you for your reply. It's been driving me crazy. I gave a lecture last week on how wonderful ggplot2 is, how much better than other graphics environments. I am scheduled to give this lecture again in a few days to a different group here at my job.

But I fear that I may mislead my audience. I am a recent convert to ggplot2. Although I've made some nice plots with it by the seat of my pants--in some cases thanks to the kindness of Hadley Wickham who has responded to my queries--I don't feel I have mastered the theory.

And I have yet to be convinced that this framework really empowers us. I am afraid that it may be just another "big collection of special cases" (Wickham 2009, page 1).

For instance: If *all* we can do with stat_qq() is make a single kind of normal quantile plot, it seems to be a very fancy, verbose version of qqnorm().  Except it is *less* powerful and *less* flexible than qqnorm(), because it does not permit us to access the ..theoretical.. and ..sample..  variables as qqnorm() does.

But I would LOVE to be shown otherwise. Someone, please show us the light.

Jake

messages.body_plain:
> Thank you for your reply. It's been driving me crazy. I gave a lecture last
> week on how wonderful ggplot2 is, how much better than other graphics
> environments. I am scheduled to give this lecture again in a few days to a
> different group here at my job.
>
> But I fear that I may mislead my audience. I am a recent convert to ggplot2.
> Although I've made some nice plots with it by the seat of my pants--in some
> cases thanks to the kindness of Hadley Wickham who has responded to my
> queries--I don't feel I have mastered the theory.

The basic problem is that the qq plot is one of the few plots that
doesn't fit well into the layered grammar of graphics. The basic
problem is that you have two layers, one point and one line, that are
both based off the same transformed dataset.  The second layer, a
line, is particularly problematical as it's a further transformation,
and depending on what your definition of a qq plots, it can be a few
different things. So it doesn't fit into the current implementation of
the grammar for two reasons:

 * you have two layers that should both be based on the same transformed dataset

 * the second layer is derived by two stages of transformations.

I have contemplated extensions to the grammar to make this possible,
and to make the definition of plots more truly hierarchical, but these
are unlikely to be implemented in the future.

Unfortunately every theory must trade elegance for coverage, and
you've narrowed on the one type of graphic that does not easily
defined in the current grammar.  I don't think this invalidates the
central idea of ggplot2 - there are still far far fewer special cases
than with other graphics systems.

Hadley

--

Department of Statistics / Rice University

messages.subject: Re: pattern fill
messages.subject_clean: pattern fill
messages.body_plain:
One approach to make fill patterns with polygons would be to use grobX
and grobY. I haven't worked out the details for parallel lines at an
angle, but it seems doable. Other patterns than lines would be more
problematic, unless we restrict the pattern to strictly inner elements
(e.g. points), because their intersection with the polygon border
would be a nightmare.

Here's an example of usage for grobX, feel free to suggest adaptations
for parallel lines,

library(grid)

g <- polygonGrob(0.1*cos(seq(0,2*pi,length=300)) +0.5,
                  0.2*sin(seq(0,2*pi,length=300))+0.5, def="npc")

gtheta <- function(g, theta){

  sapply(theta, function(.t){
         gx <- convertX(grobX(g, .t), "npc")
         gy <- convertY(grobY(g, .t), "npc")

         c(gx,gy)
       })

}

angles <- seq(10,360,by=10)
p <- gtheta(g, angles)

grid.newpage()
grid.draw(g)
grid.points(p[1,], p[2,], gp=gpar(cex=0.2),
            default.units="npc")

grid.segments(0.5,0.5, p[1,],p[2,], gp=gpar(cex=0.2),
              default.units="npc")

baptiste

messages.subject_clean: Transporting mclust() plot elements into ggplot
messages.body_plain:
Here's an attempt:
library(ellipse)
library(mclust)
library(ggplot2)

iris_mclust=Mclust(iris[,1:4])

get.ellipses <- function(coords, mclust.fit){
  centers <- mclust.fit$parameters$mean[coords, ]
  vars <- mclust.fit$parameters$variance$sigma[coords, coords, ]
  ldply(1:ncol(centers), function(cluster){
    data.frame(ellipse(vars[,,cluster], centre = centers[, cluster],
      level = 0.5), classification = cluster)
    })
}

iris.el <- get.ellipses(c("Sepal.Length", "Sepal.Width"), iris_mclust)
iris$classification <- iris_mclust$classification

ggplot(iris, aes(Sepal.Length, Sepal.Width, colour = factor(classification))) +
  geom_point(aes(shape = classification))+
  geom_path(data = iris.el,
    aes(group = classification, linetype = classification))

The size of the ellipses is the tricky part, from what I can tell
mclust uses some classification probability level. I just used the 50%
quantile for an equivalent multivariate normal (the level parameter in
ellipse).

Hope it helps,
Charlotte

messages.body_plain:
I am having a problem adding labels to specific subsets.
The code works fine if the subset is non-empty, but fails if the
subset is empty (all points are labeled).

Reproducible examples (ggplot 0.8.9, R 2.12.1 patched, Windows XP):

non-empty subset (works ok):
ggplot(mpg, aes(x=displ, y=cty, label=model)) + geom_point() +
geom_text(data=subset(mpg,cty>30/((displ/2)^0.7)),vjust=-1, size=2)

empty subset (does not work correctly, all points are labeled):
ggplot(mpg, aes(x=displ, y=cty, label=model)) + geom_point() +
geom_text(data=subset(mpg,cty>40/((displ/2)^0.7)),vjust=-1, size=2)

Right now I am going around the problem as follows, but I do not like
the solution much:
ggplot(mpg, aes(x=displ, y=cty, label=model)) + geom_point() +
(if(nrow(foo <- subset(mpg,cty>40/((displ/2)^0.7)))>0)
geom_text(data=foo, vjust=-1, size=2) else NULL)

Is there a better solution?
This problem is similar to the one mentioned in an old post present in
this forum ("Weird geom_point behavior with empty subset", Oct 19,
2009). I could not find this problem listed on github:
https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/issues.

Thanks,
Dario

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

How about this?

library(mclust)
library(ggplot2)

# iris_mclust=Mclust(iris[,1:4])

# Charlotte Wickham's function to generate ellipse coordinates

get.ellipses <- function(coords, mclust.fit){
 centers <- mclust.fit$parameters$mean[coords, ]
 vars <- mclust.fit$parameters$variance$sigma[coords, coords, ]
 ldply(1:ncol(centers), function(cluster){
   data.frame(ellipse(vars[,,cluster], centre = centers[, cluster],
     level = 0.5), classification = cluster)
   })
}

# Function to generate data frame for producing ellipses (DM)

df.ellipses <- function(mclustobj){
   # Takes an mclust object as input.
   # Outputs a data frame that contains information about ellipse
   # coordinates for all pairs of variables in the mclust object.
    require(ellipse)
    require(plyr)
    nms <- rownames(mclustobj$parameters$mean)
    n <- length(nms)
    grid <- expand.grid(x = 1:n, y = 1:n)

    grid <- subset(grid, x != y)

    grid <- cbind(grid[, 2], grid[, 1])
    ldply(1:nrow(grid), function(i){
        coords <- as.numeric(grid[i, ])
        ell <- get.ellipses(c(nms[coords]), mclustobj)
        names(ell) <- c('yval', 'xval', 'classification')
        data.frame(xvar = nms[coords[1]], yvar = nms[coords[2]], ell)
   })
}

# Brandon's plot code to graph BIC values by columns of the BIC component of
# the mclust object

orig.data<-iris[1:4]

data.mclust<-Mclust(orig.data)           # same as iris_mclust

BIC.data<-as.data.frame(data.mclust$BIC)
BIC.data$NumComp<-rownames(BIC.data)
melted.BIC<-melt(BIC.data, var.ids= "NumComp")

ggplot(melted.BIC, aes(x=as.numeric(NumComp), y=value, colour=variable, group=variable))+

   labs(x = 'Number of components', y = 'BIC', colour = '') +
# scale_x_continuous("Number of Components")+
# scale_y_continuous("BIC")+
# scale_colour_hue("")+
geom_point()+
geom_line()+
theme_bw()

# Brandon's code, slightly modified by DM, to produce a scatterplot matrix
# that includes confidence ellipses for the classifications and groupwise density
# plots along the diagonal.

mapping=aes(colour=as.factor(data.mclust$classification),
            shape=as.factor(data.mclust$classification))

grid <- expand.grid(x = 1:ncol(orig.data), y = 1:ncol(orig.data))
grid <- subset(grid, x != y)

# Data frame for plotting points in each panel
all <- ldply(1:nrow(grid), function(i) {

  xcol <- grid[i, "x"]
  ycol <- grid[i, "y"]
  data.frame(xvar = names(orig.data)[ycol], yvar = names(orig.data)[xcol],
  x = orig.data[, xcol], y = orig.data[, ycol], orig.data)
  })

all$xvar <- factor(all$xvar, levels = names(orig.data))
all$yvar <- factor(all$yvar, levels = names(orig.data))

# Data frame for plotting density estimates
densities <- ldply(1:ncol(orig.data), function(i)

       data.frame(xvar = names(orig.data)[i], yvar = names(orig.data)[i],

                  x = orig.data[, i],
                  classification = as.factor(data.mclust$classification)))

d <- ldply(1:ncol(orig.data), function(i)
       data.frame(xvar = names(orig.data)[i], x = orig.data[, i])

mapping <- defaults(mapping, aes_string(x = "x", y = "y"))
class(mapping) <- "uneval"

# Data frame for ellipse info:
u <- df.ellipses(data.mclust)

g <- ggplot(all)
g + facet_grid(xvar ~ yvar, scales = "free") +
    geom_point(map = mapping, na.rm = TRUE, size = 1.5) +
    stat_density(data = densities,
                 aes(x = x, y = ..scaled.. * diff(range(x)) + min(x),
                       colour = classification),
                 position = "identity", geom = "line", size = 1) +
    geom_path(data = u, aes(x = xval, y = yval, group = classification,
                              linetype = classification), size = 1) +
    opts(legend.position= "none")

HTH,
Dennis

messages.body_plain:
Hi Brandon:

On Wed, Feb 16, 2011 at 1:35 AM, Brandon Hurr <brando...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Dennis,
>
> That's very slick. I was wondering how to go about using Charlotte's code to run the ellipse code on the other pairs, but it makes perfect sense to put them in the scatterplot matrix. I'm wondering about a few things.
> The density plots now represent the two different clusters in the iris dataset, does this make more sense than having a representation of the entire distribution?

That's up to you; I just tried to provide an option. I just thought that if you had two groups of classifications, you might be interested in density plots for each. It's really a matter of taste, IMO...but it does explain the bimodality in the overall density plots (see example below for what I mean).

> It'd be nice to eliminate the grid object either in the top right or bottom left half of the matrix, less plotting = less CPU time and you're not really getting more information with graphs 'A' vs 'B' and 'B' vs 'A', can you put empty grid objects in a pattern like that? I've seen it done with geom_tile() for a similar correlation matrix, but that's with one plot, not multiple ones like in this instance.

I agree it's redundant. Lattice has panel functions that allow you to use one type of graphic in one off-diagonal and another type in the other. You managed to isolate the density plots along the diagonal panels; perhaps you can NA the values in the off-diagonal you don't want or set up the grid so that either x <= y or x >= y and line up df.ellipses accordingly. Let's try the idea out.

I redid the code to set the grid subset to be x < y in the initial grid and in df.ellipses() and got the following to work:

grid <- expand.grid(x = 1:ncol(orig.data), y = 1:ncol(orig.data))

grid <- subset(grid, x < y)

all <- ldply(1:nrow(grid), function(i) {
  xcol <- grid[i, "x"]
  ycol <- grid[i, "y"]
  data.frame(xvar = names(orig.data)[ycol], yvar = names(orig.data)[xcol],
  x = orig.data[, xcol], y = orig.data[, ycol], orig.data)
  })

all$xvar <- factor(all$xvar, levels = names(orig.data))
all$yvar <- factor(all$yvar, levels = names(orig.data))

u <- df.ellipses(data.mclust)

g <- ggplot(all)
g + facet_grid(xvar ~ yvar, scales = "free") +

    geom_point(map = mapping, na.rm = TRUE) +

    stat_density(aes(x = x, y = ..scaled.. * diff(range(x)) + min(x)),

#                     shape = as.factor(data.mclust$classification)),

                 data = densities, position = "identity", colour = "grey20", geom = "line") +

    geom_path(data = u, aes(x = xval, y = yval, group = classification,
                            linetype = classification), size = 1) +
    opts(legend.position= "none")

Perhaps one can generate a different data frame to produce another type of plot in the other off-diagonal and add it as a layer to the one above...

> Lastly, there's one more plot in the output of plot(Mclust()) ... "uncertainty"... which appears to be done by using scale_size and perhaps scale_alpha on geom_point() in the scatterplot. However, I'm really 'uncertain' as to where the levels for this scaling comes from.

Since I couldn't get the plot to render from data.mclust (I only got the BIC plot), I'm uncertain what you mean :)

HTH,
Dennis

I just noticed I forgot to include the modified df.ellipses() function - the only necessary change is, within the subset() statement, to replace x != y with x < y and then redefine the data frame I called u. A copy of the graph it should produce is included. I put this at the top of the previously posted code. Sorry for the inconvenience.

Dennis

df.ellipses <- function(mclustobj){

    require(ellipse)
    require(plyr)
    nms <- rownames(mclustobj$parameters$mean)
    n <- length(nms)
    grid <- expand.grid(x = 1:n, y = 1:n)

    grid <- subset(grid, x < y)                         # <<===

    grid <- cbind(grid[, 2], grid[, 1])
    ldply(1:nrow(grid), function(i){
        coords <- as.numeric(grid[i, ])
        ell <- get.ellipses(c(nms[coords]), mclustobj)
        names(ell) <- c('yval', 'xval', 'classification')
        data.frame(xvar = nms[coords[1]], yvar = nms[coords[2]], ell)
   })
}

u <- df.ellipses(data.mclust)

of simply plain red and blue squares.

as is now?
Best Regards

Lorenzo Isella

data <- rep(seq(5), 200)
tlab <- rep(c("M","F"),500)

x <- sample(data, 300)

lab <- sample(tlab, 300)

xyz <- cbind(as.data.frame(x),as.data.frame(lab))

lbls <- levels(xyz$set)
## xyz$val <- levels(xyz$val)[xyz$val]

gpl <- ggplot(xyz, aes(x=val,y=..count.., fill=set, group=set)) +
   geom_histogram(alpha=1,
                  binwidth=1,
                  origin=0.5,colour="black"
                  )+
scale_x_continuous()+
   opts(legend.text = theme_text(size = 14, vjust=0.4))+
   opts(legend.title = theme_text(size = 18,hjust=0))+
   opts(legend.position = c(0.45, 0.75),

   opts(panel.grid.minor = theme_blank())+

opts(axis.text.x = theme_text(size=15, colour="black",vjust=1))+
     opts(plot.title = theme_text(size = 25))+

opts(axis.text.y = theme_text(size=15, colour="black", hjust=1))

postscript("test.eps", width=5,height=5,horizontal = FALSE,
            onefile = FALSE, paper = "special"## ,

            )

messages.body_plain:
Hi Brandon:

Re timings:

Full set of 16 panels (10 replicates)
   user  system elapsed
   1.17    0.00    1.17

Reduced set of 10 panels (10 replicates)
   user  system elapsed
   0.62    0.01    0.64

It appears to be almost twice as fast (independent of the time it takes to render the graph in a graphics device, obviously :) The time bottleneck is the translation to the graphics device - I would expect the simpler graph to render a bit more quickly, but I doubt it will take half the time.

As for the uncertainty, it appears the sizes in the original plot are related to the 0.8 and 0.95 quantiles of the uncertainty distribution:
> with(data.mclust, sum(uncertainty > quantile(uncertainty, 0.8)))
[1] 30
> with(data.mclust, sum(uncertainty > quantile(uncertainty, 0.95)))
[1] 8
where
> quantile(data.mclust$uncertainty, c(0.8, 0.95))
         80%          95%
1.049008e-10 1.533001e-07

The range is between 0 and 0.0002; the maximum is a distinct outlier, corresponding to row 42 of the iris data.

Alas, alpha is a strictly continuous aesthetic, as far as I can tell; moreover, it has no manual scale. Size, OTOH, can be mapped to levels of an ordered factor (as shown on the on-line help page for scale_size), and I managed to get something done in that respect. The problem is that the values with the 'large' uncertainties are exclusively in class 1, and since their values are clustered more tightly together than those in class 2, there is a danger of overplotting by use of size. For that reason, I constrained it to be between 1 and 2 in the code below.

I added a 'Quantile' (ordered) factor corresponding to the relative position of the uncertainty per the above quantile scheme, and added it to data frame all. I also changed the mapping variable by adding a size aesthetic and a manual scale to set the actual sizes of the points. FInally, I pulled the scales inside the graph and made some text size adjustments in opts().

mapping=aes(colour=as.factor(all$classification),
            shape=as.factor(all$classification),
            size = all$Quantile   )

mapping <- defaults(mapping, aes_string(x = "x", y = "y"))
class(mapping) <- "uneval"

df.ellipses <- function(mclustobj){

    require(ellipse)
    require(plyr)
    nms <- rownames(mclustobj$parameters$mean)
    n <- length(nms)
    grid <- expand.grid(x = 1:n, y = 1:n)

    grid <- subset(grid, x < y)

    grid <- cbind(grid[, 2], grid[, 1])
    ldply(1:nrow(grid), function(i){
        coords <- as.numeric(grid[i, ])
        ell <- get.ellipses(c(nms[coords]), mclustobj)
        names(ell) <- c('yval', 'xval', 'classification')
        data.frame(xvar = nms[coords[1]], yvar = nms[coords[2]], ell)
   })
}

grid <- expand.grid(x = 1:ncol(orig.data), y = 1:ncol(orig.data))
grid <- subset(grid, x < y)

all <- ldply(1:nrow(grid), function(i) {
  xcol <- grid[i, "x"]
  ycol <- grid[i, "y"]
  data.frame(xvar = names(orig.data)[ycol], yvar = names(orig.data)[xcol],
  x = orig.data[, xcol], y = orig.data[, ycol],

  classification = data.mclust$classification,
  Quantile = with(data.mclust, cut(uncertainty, breaks = c(-0.01,
                  quantile(uncertainty, 0.8), quantile(uncertainty, 0.95), 0.0003),
                  labels = c('< 0.8', '0.8-0.95', '> 0.95'))))
  })

all$Quantile <- factor(all$Quantile, levels = c('< 0.8', '0.8-0.95', '> 0.95'))

all$xvar <- factor(all$xvar, levels = names(orig.data))
all$yvar <- factor(all$yvar, levels = names(orig.data))

densities <- ldply(1:ncol(orig.data), function(i)

       data.frame(xvar = names(orig.data)[i], yvar = names(orig.data)[i], x = orig.data[, i]))

u <- df.ellipses(data.mclust)

g <- ggplot(all)

g + facet_grid(xvar ~ yvar, scales = "free") + theme_bw() +

    geom_point(map = mapping, na.rm = TRUE) +

    stat_density(data = densities, aes(x = x, y = ..scaled.. * diff(range(x)) + min(x),

                                       colour = as.factor(data.mclust$classification)),

                 position = "identity", geom = "line", size = 1) +
    geom_path(data = u, aes(x = xval, y = yval, group = classification,
                            linetype = classification), size = 1) +

    labs(x = '', y = '', colour = 'Class', shape = 'Class', size = 'Quantile') +
    scale_size_manual( values = c(1, 1.5, 2) ) +
    opts(legend.position = c(0.85, 0.75),
         legend.title = theme_text(size = 12, face = 'bold'),
         legend.text = theme_text(size = 11),
         axis.text.x = theme_text(size = 8),
         axis.text.y = theme_text(size = 8) )

I wanted to change the labels for the categories by using expressions, but no can do. At least I found a way to use the extra space to position the legend inside the graph :)

Dennis

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

One of the thing I'm most proud about ggplot2 is you guys - the
ggplot2 community. I think the ggplot2 mailing list is one of the most
vibrant and useful visualisation communities on the web, and it adds a
huge amount to ggplot2.  As I apply for funding for further ggplot2
development, I'd like to be able to tell reviewers a bit more about
this group, so I'd really appreciate it if you'd complete the first
annual ggplot2 survey:

http://hadley.wufoo.com/forms/ggplot2-survey/

The more people who fill it out, the stronger the case I can make to
funding agencies, so please take a minute or two to add your data!

Thanks,

Hadley

--
Assistant Professor / Dobelman Family Junior Chair
Department of Statistics / Rice University
http://had.co.nz/

p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg))
p <- p + geom_point()

print(p)

produces a plot, but when I do this

custom_ggplot_theme<-c(theme_bw(base_size=10))
			opts(plot.title=theme_text(size=10)),
			opts(axis.text.x=theme_text(size=10, angle=90, lineheight=5)),
			opts(axis.title.x=theme_text(size=12)),
			opts(axis.text.y=theme_text(size=10)),
			opts(axis.title.y=theme_text(size=10, angle=90))
	)

p + custom_ggplot_theme

I get

Error: Don't know how to add o to a plot

According to Hadley's book I think I'm doing the right thing.  Any
ideas ?

Paul.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Hadley:

Thank you for your reply on this.

Is there a well-defined way to predict the behavior of ggplot2 syntax? I refer to something analogous to the parsing rules that govern mathematical expressions in R--or the rules that govern regular expressions in unix.

It seems that if users are to create novel graphics with ggplot2, we need to know the rules so that we can predict the result of any given syntax.

For example, consider the example offered by Luciano Selzer:

ggplot(data = DUT, aes(sample = stuff)) + stat_qq() + geom_smooth(method = "lm", aes(x = ..theoretical.., y = ..sample..), stat = "qq")

Does this parse from left to right?

Are the ..theoretical.. and ..sample.. vectors fed by the first stat_qq() call to the geom_smooth() call? If so, why does it create a *path* geometrical object rather than a *smooth*?

If it has not obtained ..theoretical.. and ..sample.. from stat_qq(), why does it not return an error saying something like "..theoretical..  not found"?

Where or how does the above syntax instruct ggplot2 to draw a path plot through the scatterplot?

The following simpler expression yields a plot almost the same as Luciano's above, but without the points:

ggplot(data = DUT, aes(sample = stuff)) + stat_qq(geom=c("path"))

whereas the following returns an error, complaining that it has not been given x and y for geom_path().

ggplot(data = DUT, aes(sample = stuff)) + stat_qq(geom=c("path")) + geom_path()

In the following, ggplot2 ignores the second geom value. Why? How would one legitimately create both a point and a path, as in traditional graphics type="o"?

ggplot(data = DUT, aes(sample = stuff)) + stat_qq(geom=c("point", "path"))

A peripheral question: Are there (or will there be) extractor functions whereby one can for instance get ..theoretical.. and ..sample.. out of a layer? For instance, consider the following object:

someObject <-ggplot(data = DUT, aes(sample = stuff)) + stat_qq(geom=c("point"))

Does someObject contain the ..theoretical.. and ..sample.. column vectors which might be extracted?

Jake Wegelin

On Mon, 14 Feb 2011, Hadley Wickham wrote:

>> Thank you for your reply. It's been driving me crazy. I gave a lecture last
>> week on how wonderful ggplot2 is, how much better than other graphics
>> environments. I am scheduled to give this lecture again in a few days to a
>> different group here at my job.
>>
>> But I fear that I may mislead my audience. I am a recent convert to ggplot2.
>> Although I've made some nice plots with it by the seat of my pants--in some
>> cases thanks to the kindness of Hadley Wickham who has responded to my
>> queries--I don't feel I have mastered the theory.
>
> The basic problem is that the qq plot is one of the few plots that
> doesn't fit well into the layered grammar of graphics. The basic
> problem is that you have two layers, one point and one line, that are
> both based off the same transformed dataset.  The second layer, a
> line, is particularly problematical as it's a further transformation,
> and depending on what your definition of a qq plots, it can be a few
> different things. So it doesn't fit into the current implementation of
> the grammar for two reasons:
>
> * you have two layers that should both be based on the same transformed dataset
>
> * the second layer is derived by two stages of transformations.
>
> I have contemplated extensions to the grammar to make this possible,
> and to make the definition of plots more truly hierarchical, but these
> are unlikely to be implemented in the future.
>
> Unfortunately every theory must trade elegance for coverage, and
> you've narrowed on the one type of graphic that does not easily
> defined in the current grammar.  I don't think this invalidates the
> central idea of ggplot2 - there are still far far fewer special cases
> than with other graphics systems.
>
> Hadley
>
> --
> Assistant Professor / Dobelman Family Junior Chair
> Department of Statistics / Rice University
> http://had.co.nz/
>

Hi Jacob,

On Wed, Feb 16, 2011 at 3:34 PM, Jacob Wegelin <jacobw...@fastmail.fm> wrote:
>
> Dear Hadley:

I'm not Hadley, but I find this stuff interesting so I hope you don't
mind if I take a shot at it.

>
> Thank you for your reply on this.
>
> Is there a well-defined way to predict the behavior of ggplot2 syntax? I
> refer to something analogous to the parsing rules that govern mathematical
> expressions in R--or the rules that govern regular expressions in unix.
>
> It seems that if users are to create novel graphics with ggplot2, we need to
> know the rules so that we can predict the result of any given syntax.

I think that creating "novel graphics" is not all that common. If a
particular kind of display has value, chances are someone has already
done it. That said, one of the great strengths of ggplot is the way it
separates the basic elements of a plot into coordinates, easthetic
mappings, geoms etc. This makes it really easy to combine different
elements -- for example I am a big fan of ploting transparent boxplots
over a dotplot, giving both a summary of a distribution as well as the
entire distribution itself.

>
> For example, consider the example offered by Luciano Selzer:
>
> ggplot(data = DUT, aes(sample = stuff)) + stat_qq() + geom_smooth(method =
> "lm", aes(x = ..theoretical.., y = ..sample..), stat = "qq")
>
> Does this parse from left to right?

Yes, in the sense that geoms added later are plotted "on top of" those
added earlier.

>
> Are the ..theoretical.. and ..sample.. vectors fed by the first stat_qq()
> call to the geom_smooth() call? If so, why does it create a *path*
> geometrical object rather than a *smooth*?

No, that is why you need stat="qq" in the geom_smooth() call.

>
> If it has not obtained ..theoretical.. and ..sample.. from stat_qq(), why
> does it not return an error saying something like "..theoretical..  not
> found"?

It has obtained them... just not from the first stat_qq() call, but
rather from the second one (the one made as a part of the
geom_smooth() call.

>
> Where or how does the above syntax instruct ggplot2 to draw a path plot
> through the scatterplot?

Basically, geom_smooth() is usually called with the default
stat="smooth", which produces a new variable y that is the predicted
value. geom_smooth() drays a line through (x, predicted_y), where x
are the observed values and predicted_y is this new variable y that is
produced by stat_smooth(). But since we changed to stat="qq", y is
still equal to sample, so the line is now drawn through the points
themselves, rather than through (x, predicted_y).

>
> The following simpler expression yields a plot almost the same as Luciano's
> above, but without the points:
>
> ggplot(data = DUT, aes(sample = stuff)) + stat_qq(geom=c("path"))

Right, because goem_path is getting the x and y coordinates from
stat_qq, which defaults to x=..theoretical.. y=..sample..

>
> whereas the following returns an error, complaining that it has not been
> given x and y for geom_path().
>
> ggplot(data = DUT, aes(sample = stuff)) + stat_qq(geom=c("path")) +
> geom_path()

Right, because it x and y have not been defined anywhere but by the
defaults to stat_qq.

>
> In the following, ggplot2 ignores the second geom value. Why? How would one
> legitimately create both a point and a path, as in traditional graphics
> type="o"?
>
> ggplot(data = DUT, aes(sample = stuff)) + stat_qq(geom=c("point", "path"))

It just doesn't work that way. Use

ggplot(data = DUT, aes(sample = stuff)) + stat_qq(geom="point") +
stat_qq(geom="path")

>
> A peripheral question: Are there (or will there be) extractor functions
> whereby one can for instance get ..theoretical.. and ..sample.. out of a
> layer? For instance, consider the following object:
>
> someObject <-ggplot(data = DUT, aes(sample = stuff)) +
> stat_qq(geom=c("point"))

Not that I know of.

>
> Does someObject contain the ..theoretical.. and ..sample.. column vectors
> which might be extracted?
>

Possibly, but I never muck around with that stuff. It's scary in there!

HTH,
Ista

> Jake Wegelin

messages.subject: Plotting on only 'half the circle' using coord_polar

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm working with some rotational data, continuous data that one might
normally summarise with a boxplot.
Because it's rotational data centered on zero with a small standard
deviation, I'm wanting to plot on the circle using polar_coord()

Here's a small example:

mydata<-data.frame(Rotation = rnorm(100,sd=10),
Group=c(rep("A",50),rep("B",50)))

ggplot(mydata,aes(x=Group,y=Rotation)) + geom_boxplot() +
coord_polar(theta="y",start=pi)+
scale_y_continuous(limits=c(-180,180),breaks=c(-180,-90,0,90,180))+
scale_x_discrete(breaks=c("","A","B",""),limits=c("","A","B",""))

You'll probably note that there are a number of weaknesses associated
with display using the polar coordinate system in this way, and I'm
trying to overcome at least two.

First, is there a way to display only the top half of the circle in
the graph - because of the small standard deviation, the bottom half
of the plot is essentially redundant.

Second, is there a better way to bring the boxplot of A and B closer
together, further towards the outside of the circle?  (Attempting to
overcome the illusion of more variation in the group closest to the
edge of the circle).  I'm using limits here, but I suspect that's not
terribly clever.

Have been puzzling over this for a while - if you've any guidance I'd
greatly appreciate it.
thanks,
Brad
