messages.body_plain:
Hi:

I managed to get a plot by simplifying (and spacing!!) the code:

> head(dat)
        date          y
1 2003-01-01 0.33943264
2 2003-02-08 0.62611516
3 2003-03-18 0.19749459
4 2003-04-26 0.30980879
5 2003-06-03 0.04741416
6 2003-07-12 0.75691885
> str(dat)
'data.frame':   20 obs. of  2 variables:
 $ date:Class 'Date'  num [1:20] 12053 12091 12130 12168 12207 ...
 $ y   : num  0.3394 0.6261 0.1975 0.3098 0.0474 ...

> blocks
  lev        ymn       ymx        xmn        xmx
1   a 0.04741416 0.0000000 2003-01-01 2005-01-01
2   b 0.00000000 0.9932042 2003-01-01 2005-01-01
> sapply(blocks, class)
      lev       ymn       ymx       xmn       xmx
 "factor" "numeric" "numeric"    "Date"    "Date"

all of which shows us that date, xmn and xmx are already Date objects and don't have to be coerced.

This gets us to
> ggplot(data=dat, aes(x=date, y=y)) +
+    geom_rect(data=blocks, aes(xmin = xmn, xmax=xmx,
+                               ymin=ymn, ymax=ymx, fill=lev))
Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos) : object 'y' not found

geom_rect() doesn't have a y argument, but you used y as an aesthetic in the base plot. This is a common gotcha - only define aesthetics in the base plot that will be present in all geoms. Removing y from the base plot aesthetic list renders a plot:

ggplot(data=dat, aes(x=date)) +
    geom_rect(data=blocks, aes(xmin = xmn, xmax=xmx,
                               ymin=ymn, ymax=ymx, fill=lev))

When you look at the two sets of x extremes in the blocks data frame, you can see they're the same, so the second overwrites the first. You can also see that your ymn at level a is higher than the max, so you still have a problem.

Let's add a lev factor to the original data frame for the purposes of illustration and use the ddply() function from plyr to get summaries:

dat2 <- dat
dat2$lev <- rep(c('a', 'b'), each = 10)
blocks <- ddply(dat2, 'lev', summarise, ymn = min(0, min(y)), ymx = max(0, max(y)),
                         xmn = min(date), xmx = max(date))
> blocks
  lev ymn       ymx        xmn        xmx
1   a   0 0.9734301 2003-01-01 2003-12-13
2   b   0 0.9932042 2004-01-20 2005-01-01

ggplot(data=dat2, aes(x=date)) +
   geom_rect(data=blocks, aes(xmin = xmn, xmax=xmx,
                              ymin=ymn, ymax=ymx, fill=lev), alpha = 0.3)

Hmm, probably not quite what you wanted. For this type of color split, it's better to let the y-ranges be infinite (or at least the same), and use the mean date (which just happens to be New Year's Day 2004 in this example, fortunately) to separate the x-ranges of the rectangles. Notice I'm also using alpha transparency to mute the background color. It would also make sense to plot a time series, so that's included below.

Reading between the lines, perhaps you were aiming for something like this. Notice that I'm defining the rectangle boundaries rather than summarizing them, as it provides more control.

blocks2 <- data.frame(lev = c('a', 'b'), ymn = -Inf, ymx = Inf,
                      xmn = c(min(dat2$date), mean(dat2$date)),
                      xmx = c(mean(dat2$date), max(dat2$date)))

# Notice how xmx for level a aligns with xmn for level b
> blocks2
  lev  ymn ymx        xmn        xmx
1   a -Inf Inf 2003-01-01 2004-01-01
2   b -Inf Inf 2004-01-01 2005-01-01

# Plot with a time series (we might as well use y since we went to
# the trouble of defining it :)
ggplot(data=dat2, aes(x=date)) + labs(fill = 'Level', linetype = 'Level') +
   geom_line(aes(y = y, linetype = lev), size = 1) +
   geom_rect(data=blocks2, aes(xmin = xmn, xmax=xmx,
                              ymin=ymn, ymax=ymx, fill=lev), alpha = 0.3)

You had the right idea by using a separate data frame to provide the appropriate inputs to geom_rect(), but the errors in this case are instructive and hopefully you have learned a couple of useful tricks. (For example, why did assigning Level to be the legend title for both fill and linetype work? What happens if you remove one?)

Cheers,
Dennis

messages.subject: Re: How to visualize clusters on heatmap
messages.subject_clean: How to visualize clusters on heatmap
messages.body_plain:
Dear San,

Clustering can be a quite complex task, there are tons of publications
on that and even entire R package, depending which algorithm You want
to use and how You want to define clusters. This is complex topic I
don't think ggplot2 which is a graphic drawing library is implementing
anything like that.

There is kmeans algorithm which you might want to use
http://www.r-chart.com/2010/09/bot-botany-k-means-and-ggplot2.html
After You cluster Your data, You might want to arrange them correctly
on the heatmap by scale_x_discrete(...) and scale_y_discrete(...) for
that You can refer to very good example on
http://theatavism.blogspot.com/2009/05/plotting-correlation-matrix-with.html

For a dendogram in ggplot2 You might want to look at
http://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/4062/how-to-plot-a-fan-polar-dendrogram-in-r
and then maybe just use different coord system.

I hope this helps :) I did correlation map but never tried any
clusters visualization yet. I might be interested in that in a couple
of days.
There is also this "NeatMap" package for R using ggplot2, but I
haven't looked into it yet.

Hey Group,

I am trying to plot two sets of points using two colors. The second
set is much smaller than the first set, so when I plot them, we cannot
really see the second set among all the points. Here is an example

library("ggplot2")
N1 <- 10000
N2 <- 10
myData1 <- data.frame(x=
rnorm(N1,6,3),y=runif(N1),condition=rep("treatment",N1))
myData2 <- data.frame(x= rnorm(N2,6,3),y=runif(N2),condition=rep("control",N2))
allData <- rbind(myData1,myData2)

library(ggplot2)
p <- ggplot(allData,aes(x=x,y=y,colour=factor(condition)))
p <-  p + geom_point()
p

To work around this, I used layers. But then I lose the legend
indicating what the color corresponds to.

library(ggplot2)
p <- ggplot(myData1,aes(x=x,y=y))
p <- p + geom_point(alpha=0.1)
p <- p + layer(data=myData2,mapping=aes(x=x,y=y),geom='point',colour='red')
p

Any suggestions on how to improve my plot. Thanks!

Juliet

messages.subject: Re: barplot with secondary y axis
messages.subject_clean: barplot with secondary y axis
messages.body_plain:
Luciano-

What you're trying to do (2, differently scaled axes) is not supported
in ggplot2 and is generally not considered a good idea, although it's
a popular question both here and elsewhere. I work with Brian, and
you're correct about what we're doing: 2 axes, where the axes are
simply transformations, such as miles to kilometers or pounds to
kilograms. That's still hard to do in ggplot2, but doesn't violate the
semantics of "Grammar of Graphics", which ggplot2 implements [ see
http://www.google.com/search?q=grammer+of+graphics ]

What you're asking to do breaks the underlying semantics and is widely
discourage for visualizations [ see http://tomhopper.wordpress.com/2010/08/30/graphing-highly-skewed-data/
and http://www.google.com/search?q=Stephen+Few+dual+scaled+axes ].

-Wil

If I'm understanding you correctly, then luciano's reply seems

base graphics will certainly let you construct dual y axes (by hand,
essentially) if you like. The reason (to the best of my knowledge)
that this is not possible in ggplot is that dual y axes are generally
considered a very, very bad idea. They are often confusing and can be
made to say nearly anything you like.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Joran,

I could not come up with a nice way to do what you wanted off the top
of my head, but is this acceptable?  I know it is not quite what you
asked for...

###############
require(ggplot2)
em <- melt(economics, id = "date")
mylabs <- paste("Y Label", 1:5)
em$variable <- factor(em$variable, labels = mylabs)
qplot(date, value, data = em, geom = "line", group = variable) +
  facet_grid(variable ~ ., scale = "free_y") + ylab(NULL)
###############

Best regards,

Josh

g2 = gTree(children = gList(g), cl=c("arrange", "ggplot"))
print.arrange = function(x, ...) grid.draw(x)

ggsave("test.pdf", g2)

Just a thought anyway,

baptiste

messages.subject: Re: Separate y-axis titles when faceting using scales="free_y"
messages.subject_clean: Separate y-axis titles when faceting using scales="free_y"
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

To place the facet titles on the left side and mimic titles, you could try this,

library(ggplot2)
library(gridExtra)

em <- melt(economics, id = "date")
mylabs <- paste("Y Label", 1:5)
em$variable <- factor(em$variable, labels = mylabs)

p <-

qplot(date, value, data = em, geom = "line", group = variable) +
 facet_grid(variable ~ ., scale = "free_y") + ylab(NULL)

labs <- llply(levels(em$variable), textGrob, rot=90)

## add a blank grob "sub" below, as the y title is aligned with the full
## ggplot2 height, not just the panel

my.labels <-
  do.call(arrangeGrob,
          c(labs, list(ncol=1, left="My y title", sub="")))

## grid.draw(my.labels)

## hack: define the width of my.labels
ylab <- gTree(children=gList(my.labels),
              cl="mylabels" )

widthDetails.mylabels <- function(x)
  max(stringHeight(levels(em$variable))) + unit(1, "line")

## hack: tweak ggplot2's axis.title.y option to use our gTree
foo <- function()
  function(label, x, y) ylab

p + opts(strip.text.y =theme_blank(),
         strip.background=theme_blank()) +
         opts(  axis.title.y = foo())

HTH,

baptiste

messages.subject: Re: barplot with secondary y axis
messages.subject_clean: barplot with secondary y axis
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Let me reinforce Joran's observation. Hadley is on record in the list archives saying that he doesn't support multiple axis scaling in ggplot2, a stance that I applaud. (I mean those situations where one wants to plot u vs. v and x vs. y in the same graphics region with the two [often unrelated] sets of scales populating opposite sides of their corresponding axis.) Excel lets you be as bad as you wanna be - OTOH, R's graphics systems make it difficult for you to perform bad graphics, but not impossible. That's a feature, not a bug. However, I do have some sympathy with those who would like to use related scales in different units (e.g., euros vs. USD, lb. vs. kg), as shown in one of the links referenced earlier in this thread.

Having said that, if you *really* want that double scaled plot, look to the twoord.plot() function in package plotrix, which works with the base graphics system.

Dennis

I've just committed a change to grid.arrange() that should detect the
presence of a ggplot and make the output compatible with ggsave.

library(ggplot2)
source("http://gridextra.googlecode.com/svn/trunk/R/arrange.r")

g1 = rectGrob(gp=gpar(fill="grey"))
g2 = textGrob("test")
g3 = qplot(1:10, 1:10)

grid.arrange(g1,g2,g3)

g4 = arrangeGrob(g1,g2,g3, main = "testing grid.arrange()")
g5 = arrangeGrob(g1,g2), main = "testing grid.arrange()")

ggsave("test.pdf", g4)

## this fails, no ggplot present
ggsave("test2.pdf", g5)
# Error in ggsave("test2.pdf", g5) : plot should be a ggplot2 plot

baptiste

messages.subject: drop=FALSE not working in facet_wrap()? bug in plyr::split_labels?
messages.subject_clean: drop=FALSE not working in facet_wrap()? bug in plyr::split_labels?
messages.body_plain:
I was trying to respond to

<http://stackoverflow.com/questions/5036938/include-unused-factor-levels-in-facets-with-ggplot2>

  where the questioner wants to know if there is a way to reserve space
for unused levels in a faceted plot.  From the graph he shows, he is
stretching the ggplot idiom a little bit -- what he wants might work
better in facet_grid, where space is left fo empty *combinations* of
levels, but he seems to be arranging plots of different variables with
different color schemes in three rows (with grid.arrange() or something).

  According to the documentation for facet_wrap(), the drop=FALSE
argument should do this, but it didn't seem to work.

     # By default, any empty factor levels will be dropped
     mpg$cyl2 <- factor(mpg$cyl, levels = c(2, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10))
     qplot(displ, hwy, data = mpg) + facet_wrap(~ cyl2)
     # Use drop = FALSE to force their inclusion
     qplot(displ, hwy, data = mpg) + facet_wrap(~ cyl2, drop = FALSE)

  I have a dug in a little way to see if there is some obvious small
bug, but I can't see how this was supposed to work.

 From facet-wrap.r:

  # Data shape
  initialise <- function(., data) {
    # Compute facetting variables for all layers
    vars <- ldply(data, function(df) {
      as.data.frame(eval.quoted(.$facets, df))
    })

    .$facet_levels <- split_labels(vars, .$drop)
    .$facet_levels$PANEL <- factor(1:nrow(.$facet_levels))
  }

  I checked to see that '.$drop' was in fact FALSE when we got inside
this function ...

  OK, so the facet levels are obtained via split_labels(), which is in plyr:

function (splits, drop, id = plyr::id(splits, drop = TRUE))
{
    if (length(splits) == 0)
        return(data.frame())
    if (drop) {
        representative <- which(!duplicated(id))[order(unique(id))]
        quickdf(lapply(splits, function(x) x[representative]))
    }
    else {
        unique_values <- llply(splits, function(x) sort(unique(x)))
        names(unique_values) <- names(splits)
        rev(expand.grid(rev(unique_values), stringsAsFactors = FALSE))
    }
}

  I can't see how this was supposed to work. plyr is using expand.grid()
from base R, but I see no evidence that expand.grid() uses (or is
supposed to use?) the *levels* of the factor it is given rather than the
*values* it is given.  Was this previously true?

  I would have thought these were supposed to give different answers:

> split_labels(factor("A",levels=c("A","B")),drop=TRUE)
  Var1
1    A
> split_labels(factor("A",levels=c("A","B")),drop=TRUE)
  X1
1  A

  (There is also a small typo in the documentation for plyr: the
description of the arguments is mangled ...)

  Does anyone have any thoughts?

R 2.12.1, ggplot2_0.8.9, plyr_1.4

messages.body_plain:
William, I know about that and I agree that it can be very confusing. I was just answering Max's question.
Luciano

2011/2/18 William Doane <w...@drdoane.com>

> Luciano-
>
> What you're trying to do (2, differently scaled axes) is not supported
> in ggplot2 and is generally not considered a good idea, although it's
> a popular question both here and elsewhere. I work with Brian, and
> you're correct about what we're doing: 2 axes, where the axes are
> simply transformations, such as miles to kilometers or pounds to
> kilograms. That's still hard to do in ggplot2, but doesn't violate the
> semantics of "Grammar of Graphics", which ggplot2 implements [ see
> http://www.google.com/search?q=grammer+of+graphics ]
>

messages.body_plain:
Hi thomas-

One pleasant thing would be to include all your library calls at the top. I had discover that I had to install several libraries in an iterative manner....

the wc.txt file you supplied, and which I renamed world_counted.txt, has errors (extra comma in country names) on 3 lines 196,205,228. These cause errors in world.ggmape$y2007 which you could have discovered by
str(world.ggmape) and wondering why y2007 is a factor with a first level even shown of "deomocratic...." then you could have done a table(world.ggmape$y2007) to get perhaps a more clear view of what happened. next you might have printed elect.gen.tot to see the issues there. just some suggestions on how to trouble shoot this.

because y2007 was interpreted as a factor due to inclusion of , you have 112 levels in the color legend in your first plot. note how they were sorted too. when you convert factors to continuous you only get the factor index which in this case is less than 112, why everything looks like 0 in that scale range. you have to convert factors to numeric via numeric=as.numeric(as.character(factor)).

anyway, fixing the input file, you get a variable that is properly typed as integer and a map which is colored showing basically the US, phillipines, and west germany as having more y2007 than almost all other regions with the US way higher than these others. So, I think I'm getting your desired output. Just run your original example after fixing the input file.

Cheers,
James

One way around the limit of scale_fill_brewer is to use scale_fill_manual and repeat the Color Brewer colors, e.g:

scale_fill_manual(values=rep(RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(12, "Set3"), 5))

With so many colors you're going to end up with similar colors anyways, but at least this way any group of 12 adjacent colors will be distinct.

messages.body_plain:
Everyone,

That was quick work. I really like the idea of the pairs plot with density estimations along the diagonal. I think I like it with the density plots separated by group. If they were together there is the potential of a bulbous blob of a distribution even if you have clear groups within the data, depending on the kernel adjustment being used. With them separated you can more easily interpret whether the distributions look separated or are close enough together to be from a single distribution.

Is there a way to draw the dotted lines within the ellipses? I don't see it in the ellipse() manual?

My guess, as far as the uncertainty plot goes, is that the point size is based on the $uncertainty value returned from Mclust(). There are never more than three sizes of dots so it must be binning them. I would assume it's binning based on three st. devs. from the mean of the encertainties but that is just a guess. The uncertainty numbers for the iris dataset are incredibly small, I'm not really sure what they represent. They are also fairly obviously not normally distributed, with all those zeros I would say I'd fit it with an exponential distribution but I'm not expert.  Sorry I'm not more help.

Jens

messages.body_plain:
I'm guessing you'd have to do them with abline, but I think that would be quite complex as you'd have to compute the line equation from the mean center and the shortest and fatest point of the ellipse, the intersects of the lines with the ellipse. Perhaps there's an easier way, but I don't know of it.

B

If they were together there is the potential of a bulbous blob of a distribution even if you have clear groups within the data, depending on the kernel adjustment being used. With them separated you can more easily interpret whether the distributions look separated or are close enough together to be from a single distribution.
>
> Is there a way to draw the dotted lines within the ellipses? I don't see it in the ellipse() manual?
>
> My guess, as far as the uncertainty plot goes, is that the point size is based on the $uncertainty value returned from Mclust(). There are never more than three sizes of dots so it must be binning them. I would assume it's binning based on three st. devs. from the mean of the encertainties but that is just a guess. The uncertainty numbers for the iris dataset are incredibly small, I'm not really sure what they represent. They are also fairly obviously not normally distributed, with all those zeros I would say I'd fit it with an exponential distribution but I'm not expert.  Sorry I'm not more help.

messages.subject: Re: pattern fill
messages.subject_clean: pattern fill
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I agree that colours look nicer than different shades of grey and I
also agree that the problem with colour blindness can easily be
avoided by checking for the right colours. However, there are some
good reasons why black and white patterns would be a huge improvement
for ggplot2. Almost a third (ca. 10 out of 33) of the geoms uses an
area that could be filled with a colour or a pattern. To publish a
nice coloured graph in a journal can cost up to several hundred Euros
per graph, which is not really cheap in my view. In some journals
coloured graphs can be published for free electronically but will be
printed in black and white if the authors don’t pay for the coloured
graphs. But even if graphs are published in colour electronically and
in print there still remains the problem that e.g. a librarian might
copy it in black and white at an article request which in the worst
case makes a graph useless. Different shades of grey are a good
alternative but only for a very limited number of colours/shades. The
most robust and basic solution for all these problems would be simple
black and white patterns. Only problem: they should not look stupid or
clumsy like in Excel but I’m sure there are some nice patterns
available. So if anyone could implement black and white patterns into
the next version of ggplot I would be really grateful and happy and I
think the same would apply to many other people as well.

Best wishes,

Martin

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I'm developing a package that makes heavy use of ggplot2. I've created my own geom—geom_rug_alt—as a way of putting rug fringes on the top/right of the plot instead of the default locations.

My problem is that when geom_rug_alt() is defined and called within a single script <https://gist.github.com/836059>, it seems to plot just fine. (Please try it yourself to verify that.) But, in my package geom_rug_alt() is defined in one file (CommonFunctions.R) and called in another (the "Residuals()" function of larger function foo.R). When I call foo.R on something, I get this error:

Error in geom_rug_alt(aes(x = NULL, y = within.group.residuals, color = factor(within.1.sd.of.the.mean.of.all.residuals)),  :

  object 'GeomRugAlt' not found

Now, I've done a couple of things (suggested by Hadley in this thread <https://groups.google.com/d/topic/ggplot2/uNjqUHkms8M/discussion>) to try to make sure that geom_rug_alt() should work properly within the package:
I define GeomRugAlt as a proto object in a file essentially called CommonFunctions.R within my package. CommonFunctions.R contains lines 3-42 of my example script <https://gist.github.com/836059>.
In CommonFunctions.R, I was sure to include the build_accessor() line for geom_rug_alt (line 42 in my example script <https://gist.github.com/836059>) after the definition of GeomRugAlt
In the package DESCRIPTION file, I have a "collate:" line where CommonFunctions.R appears first
In the package DESCRIPTION file, I have a "LazyLoad: false" line
In CommonFunctions.R, I included a require("ggplot2") call before defining GeomRugAlt as a proto object.
In foo.R, I included a require("ggplot2") call before calling geom_rug_alt() within Residuals().
I'm not sure what else I'm missing. Given that my example script <https://gist.github.com/836059> runs just fine, I suspect the issue isn't that my geom doesn't work, but that I'm doing something wrong as part of the package development process.

- Brian

messages.subject_clean: unused combinations in facet_grid
messages.body_plain:
The facet_grid documentation seems to imply that a panel is created for every combination of factors, whether data for it exists or not.

And the example below appears to illustrate this:

tst<-data.frame(region=c("a","a","b","b","b","c"),district=c("a1","a2","b1","b2","b3","c1"),percent=c(.1,.3,.2,.25,.35,.23))
ggplot(tst,aes(district,percent))+
  geom_bar(position="dodge",alpha=.3,aes(fill=district))+
  facet_grid(region~.,scales="free",space="free")+
  coord_flip()+
  opts(legend.position="none")+
  scale_y_continuous(formatter="percent")

However, there's an example in the facet_grid documentation that excludes combinations with no data (every model of car has just one manufacturer):

# Free scales are particularly useful for categorical variables
qplot(cty, model, data=mpg) +
 facet_grid(manufacturer ~ ., scales = "free", space = "free")

So is it possible to exclude the panels of missing data or not? And if so, why does the first example not do so, but the second does? Thanks very much for your help.

Adam Loveland

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

This works, but it's a vertical bar plot rather than a horizontal one. It has to do with the way that the facet_grid() is set up. Unfortunately, when you coord_flip() this, the coordinates get flipped but the faceting does not...the result is pretty ugly. That the faceting does not flip is key to the outcome.

ggplot(tst,aes(district, percent))+
  geom_bar(aes(fill = district), alpha = 0.3, position = 'dodge')+
  facet_grid(. ~ region, scales="free", space = 'free')+
 # coord_flip()+

  opts(legend.position="none")+
  scale_y_continuous(formatter="percent")

Notice that the book example did not have a coord_flip() layer; it matters. You can use position = dodge with space = 'free' in the facet_grid() statement as long as the bar charts are in sync with the faceting variable before the coord_flip() takes place (which of course makes coord_flip() pointless...)

If you flip district and percent as follows:

ggplot(tst,aes(percent, district))+
  geom_bar(aes(fill = district), alpha = 0.3, position = 'dodge')+
  facet_grid(region ~ ., scales="free", space = 'free')+
 # coord_flip()+
  opts(legend.position="none")+
  scale_x_continuous(formatter="percent")

you'll see that the levels are correct on the vertical scale because they're in sync with the faceting variable, but geom_bar() uses the y-coordinate for the count/percent/proportion, so that's why the result looks the way it does. geom_bar() is behaving as documented.

The reason your plot does not abridge levels is because the original bar charts were not in sync with the faceting variable *before* the coord_flip(). coord_flip() will flip the x and y axes *in each panel*, but it will not flip the faceting arrangement, and that is why the vertical bar plots work in this example while the horizontal ones do not.

HTH,
Dennis

  scale_x_continuous(formatter="percent")

you'll see that the levels are correct on the vertical scale because they're in sync with the faceting variable, but geom_bar() uses the y-coordinate for the count/percent/proportion, so that's why the result looks the way it does. geom_bar() is behaving as documented.

The reason your plot does not abridge levels is because the original bar charts were not in sync with the faceting variable *before* the coord_flip(). coord_flip() will flip the x and y axes *in each panel*, but it will not flip the faceting arrangement, and that is why the vertical bar plots work in this example while the horizontal ones do not.

HTH,
Dennis

On Sun, Feb 20, 2011 at 9:01 AM, <Adam_L...@keybank.com> wrote:

The facet_grid documentation seems to imply that a panel is created for every combination of factors, whether data for it exists or not.

And the example below appears to illustrate this:

tst<-data.frame(region=c("a","a","b","b","b","c"),district=c("a1","a2","b1","b2","b3","c1"),percent=c(.1,.3,.2,.25,.35,.23))
ggplot(tst,aes(district,percent))+
  geom_bar(position="dodge",alpha=.3,aes(fill=district))+
  facet_grid(region~.,scales="free",space="free")+
  coord_flip()+
  opts(legend.position="none")+
  scale_y_continuous(formatter="percent")

However, there's an example in the facet_grid documentation that excludes combinations with no data (every model of car has just one manufacturer):

# Free scales are particularly useful for categorical variables
qplot(cty, model, data=mpg) +
 facet_grid(manufacturer ~ ., scales = "free", space = "free")

So is it possible to exclude the panels of missing data or not? And if so, why does the first example not do so, but the second does? Thanks very much for your help.

Adam Loveland

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

On Sun, Feb 20, 2011 at 4:24 PM, <Adam_L...@keybank.com> wrote:
>
> Thank you Dennis and Brandon! Thanks for the clarification. I guess I'll use points. It does seem strange the way the bar_plot  behaves when the y-axis is designated for the categorical variable (as opposed to its behavior when coord_flip is used, faceting aside).

It's not 'strange' - it's documented behavior. Look carefully at the help page of geom_bar - its required aesthetic is *x*. Unlike base or lattice, there is no analogous option for horizontal = TRUE. The output from stat_bin - whether count, percentage or proportion - is the y, and it is numeric. That is the implementation. coord_flip() interchanges the x and y axes within a panel - it does not flip facets at the same time.

You can also use geom_segment() to connect points to a designated axis; in fact, there is an example of it at the bottom of the on-line help page for geom_segment(). The size aesthetic controls the thickness of the segment, so you can manufacture it into the equivalent of a horizontal bar plot. Using your example data,

tst<-data.frame(region=c("a","a","b","b","b","c"),
                district=c("a1","a2","b1","b2","b3","c1"),
                percent=c(.1,.3,.2,.25,.35,.23))

g <- ggplot(tst, aes(x = percent, y= district)
g + geom_segment(aes(colour = district,
                     yend = district, xend = 0),
                 size = 20, alpha = 0.3) +
    theme_bw() +
    facet_grid(region ~ ., scales = 'free', space = 'free') +
    scale_x_continuous(formatter = 'percent') +
    opts(legend.position = 'none')

HTH,
Dennis

Dear ggploters,

I am trying to plot two insets on a ggplot, where the insets are
phylogenetic trees of species. The below example uses the ggplot2
economics dataset, and I generate two random trees. Is there a way to
add foreign plot types as insets on ggplots?

################
require(ape)
require(ggplot2)
data(economics)

(b <- qplot(uempmed, unemploy, data = economics) +
  geom_smooth(se = F))

tree1 <- rtree(20) # generate random tree of 20 species
tree2 <- rtree(20) # generate another random tree of 20 species
plot(tree1) # visualize tree 1
plot(tree2) # visualize tree 2

# Trying to plot these trees does not work. "print" in package ape
just prints the tree to the console
subvp1 <- viewport(width = 0.4, height = 0.4, x = 0.75, y = 0.35)
subvp2 <- viewport(width = 0.4, height = 0.4, x = 0.35, y = 0.75)
b
print(tree1, vp = subvp1)
print(tree2, vp = subvp2)

Thanks! Scott

Hi Tiannan,

I would seriously question whether 360 gridlines and tick marks is a
good idea  It is liable to be difficult to see the individual ones
(unless you have a really big graph).  Nevertheless:

require(ggplot2)
dfrm <- data.frame(x = 1:360, y = runif(360))
ggplot(data = dfrm, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point() +
## I specified the default labels, you could change them
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:360, labels = 1:360)

Cheers,

Josh

messages.subject_clean: Basic question about data orientation along x axis
messages.body_plain:
Hi Art,

The easiest trick (I think) is to just (re)factor the variable so that
the order of the levels corresponds to what you want (in this case,
the same order as they appear).  Here is example code:

## Read your data in
jenn <- read.table(textConnection("

     X   DM   DI   DL   VM   VI   VL
1   r1  2.7  6.8  6.5  2.5  7.3  5.0
2 r2.5  2.7 10.8 10.5  2.7  8.5 10.2
3 r2.5  9.5 16.5  9.7  7.3 13.2 10.7
4   r3 13.2 42.7 20.7  9.2 26.0 20.0
5   r4 17.7 49.2 27.5  6.3 35.7 26.5
6   i1 36.2 40.3 30.2 10.0 37.0 19.5
7   i2 52.0 34.2 20.3 34.0 36.0 25.5
8   i3 45.0 58.0 25.3 29.3 49.2 32.7

9   c1 32.3 44.3 16.2 23.5 42.7 22.3"), header = TRUE)
closeAllConnections()
str(jenn)
levels(jenn$X)

## Graph
ggplot(jenn, aes(X, DL)) + geom_point()

## factor so that levels are in order, not alphabetical
jenn$X <- factor(jenn$X, levels = jenn$X, labels = jenn$X)

levels(jenn$X)
## New Graph
ggplot(jenn, aes(X, DL)) + geom_point()

Cheers,

Josh

messages.body_plain:
Hi Art,

Unfortunately, you cannot quite use your "X" column as the rownames
(as in mtcars) because it is not unique.  One of the requirements (in
R) for rownames is that they be unique.  For example, if you asked for
row "r2.5", which one should R give you?  Say you made them unique
using r2 and r2.5, the following would work:

## Read your data in
jenn <- read.table(textConnection("

     X   DM   DI   DL   VM   VI   VL
1   r1  2.7  6.8  6.5  2.5  7.3  5.0
2 r2  2.7 10.8 10.5  2.7  8.5 10.2

3 r2.5  9.5 16.5  9.7  7.3 13.2 10.7
4   r3 13.2 42.7 20.7  9.2 26.0 20.0
5   r4 17.7 49.2 27.5  6.3 35.7 26.5
6   i1 36.2 40.3 30.2 10.0 37.0 19.5
7   i2 52.0 34.2 20.3 34.0 36.0 25.5
8   i3 45.0 58.0 25.3 29.3 49.2 32.7
9   c1 32.3 44.3 16.2 23.5 42.7 22.3"), header = TRUE)
closeAllConnections()

## overwrite default rownames
rownames(jenn) <- jenn$X
jenn <- jenn[, -1] # 'remove' column 1, "X"

## A possible plot
ggplot(jenn, aes(DM, DL, colour = rownames(jenn))) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_colour_hue(name = "Rows")

## at this point, you can access specific rows via indexing (see ?"[" )
jenn["c1", 2:4] # row "c1" columns 2 through 4

Cheers,

Josh

messages.body_plain:
Adam,

Should work just fine.  You just define the levels of your factor and then plot. Because you're faceting by one factor and then reorganizing another as well you won't see b1 before a1 unless region b is before region a.

tst<-data.frame(region=c("a","a","b","b","b","c"),district=c("a1","a2","b1","b2","b3","c1"),percent=c(.1,.3,.2,.25,.35,.23))

tst$region<-factor(tst$region, levels=c("c", "a", "b"))
tst$district<-factor(tst$district, levels=c("b1","a2","b3","b2","a1","c1"))

ggplot(tst,aes(percent,district))+
geom_point()+
facet_grid(region~.,scales="free",space="free")+
opts(legend.position="none")+

scale_x_continuous(formatter="percent")       #scale_y was incorrect

#B

messages.subject: Re: scale_colour_grey and name
messages.subject_clean: scale_colour_grey and name
messages.body_plain:
I just came across this while trying to do a similar problem, searched
the boards and found this post so I'll reply to it.

The issue here is that scale_grey works on a sequential (discrete)
scale as opposed to a continuous one.  So when it gets a continuous
variable, it errors just like scale_shape would. (Which turns out to
be a bad example because, in a bizarre turn of events, scale_shape
works with continuous variables.  Try running qplot(1:10, 1:10, shape
= rnorm(10)) .)  I always thought that the grey scale was a kind of
simplified wrapper for scale_gradient(low = 'black', high = 'white');
is there a reason why it forces a discrete scale?

messages.subject: Re: drop=FALSE not working in facet_wrap()? bug in plyr::split_labels?
messages.subject_clean: drop=FALSE not working in facet_wrap()? bug in plyr::split_labels?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben,

In the NEWS for plyr 1.5 (unreleased):

* `split_labels` correctly preserves empty factor levels, which means that
  `drop = FALSE` should work in more places. Use `base::droplevels` to remove
  levels that don't occur in the data, and `drop = T` to remove combinations
  of levels that don't occur.

I suspect that fixes the bug.

Hadley

On Fri, Feb 18, 2011 at 8:33 AM, Ben Bolker <bbo...@gmail.com> wrote:
>  I was trying to respond to
>
> <http://stackoverflow.com/questions/5036938/include-unused-factor-levels-in-facets-with-ggplot2>
>
>  where the questioner wants to know if there is a way to reserve space
> for unused levels in a faceted plot.  From the graph he shows, he is
> stretching the ggplot idiom a little bit -- what he wants might work
> better in facet_grid, where space is left fo empty *combinations* of
> levels, but he seems to be arranging plots of different variables with
> different color schemes in three rows (with grid.arrange() or something).
>
>  According to the documentation for facet_wrap(), the drop=FALSE
> argument should do this, but it didn't seem to work.
>
>     # By default, any empty factor levels will be dropped
>     mpg$cyl2 <- factor(mpg$cyl, levels = c(2, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10))
>     qplot(displ, hwy, data = mpg) + facet_wrap(~ cyl2)
>     # Use drop = FALSE to force their inclusion
>     qplot(displ, hwy, data = mpg) + facet_wrap(~ cyl2, drop = FALSE)
>
>
>  I have a dug in a little way to see if there is some obvious small
> bug, but I can't see how this was supposed to work.
>
>  From facet-wrap.r:
>
>  # Data shape
>  initialise <- function(., data) {
>    # Compute facetting variables for all layers
>    vars <- ldply(data, function(df) {
>      as.data.frame(eval.quoted(.$facets, df))
>    })
>
>    .$facet_levels <- split_labels(vars, .$drop)
>    .$facet_levels$PANEL <- factor(1:nrow(.$facet_levels))
>  }
>
>
>  I checked to see that '.$drop' was in fact FALSE when we got inside
> this function ...
>
>  OK, so the facet levels are obtained via split_labels(), which is in plyr:
>
> function (splits, drop, id = plyr::id(splits, drop = TRUE))
> {
>    if (length(splits) == 0)
>        return(data.frame())
>    if (drop) {
>        representative <- which(!duplicated(id))[order(unique(id))]
>        quickdf(lapply(splits, function(x) x[representative]))
>    }
>    else {
>        unique_values <- llply(splits, function(x) sort(unique(x)))
>        names(unique_values) <- names(splits)
>        rev(expand.grid(rev(unique_values), stringsAsFactors = FALSE))
>    }
> }
>
>  I can't see how this was supposed to work. plyr is using expand.grid()
> from base R, but I see no evidence that expand.grid() uses (or is
> supposed to use?) the *levels* of the factor it is given rather than the
> *values* it is given.  Was this previously true?
>
>  I would have thought these were supposed to give different answers:
>
>> split_labels(factor("A",levels=c("A","B")),drop=TRUE)
>  Var1
> 1    A
>> split_labels(factor("A",levels=c("A","B")),drop=TRUE)
>  X1
> 1  A
>
>  (There is also a small typo in the documentation for plyr: the
> description of the arguments is mangled ...)
>
>  Does anyone have any thoughts?
>
> R 2.12.1, ggplot2_0.8.9, plyr_1.4
>

messages.subject: aligning plots with ggExtra align.plots(): problems
messages.subject_clean: aligning plots with ggExtra align.plots(): problems
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I do many analyses on timeseries data where want to look at many different vectors with the same time axis.   Due to various restrictions in the way one can mix and match a dataset I need to be able to align multiple ggplots vertically with precise x axis alignment.

the ggExtra  align.plots() function only works in the most trivial cases (i think).   For instance consider the following plots:

Da <- rbind(
data.frame(t=seq(1,100), var=rnorm(100), type='This is a test'),
data.frame(t=seq(1,100), var=rnorm(100), type='A'))

Db <- rbind(
data.frame(t=seq(1,100), var=rnorm(100), type='A'),
data.frame(t=seq(1,100), var=rnorm(100), type='B'))

Dc <- data.frame(t=seq(1,100), star=rnorm(100), type='A')

Ga <- ggplot() + geom_line(aes(x=t,y=var,colour=type), data=Da)
Gb1 <- ggplot() + geom_line(aes(x=t,y=var,colour=type), data=Db)
Gb2 <- ggplot() + geom_line(aes(x=t,y=var,colour=type), data=Db) + facet_grid(type ~ .)

Gc <- ggplot() + geom_line(aes(x=t,y=star, colour=type), data=Dc)

library(ggExtra)
align.plots (Gc, Ga)   # this is not aligned due to diff in legend width
align.plots (Gc, Gb1) # this aligns as legend width ~same
align.plots (Gc, Gb2) # this does not align as facet decoration not accounted for

Only 1 of the above plots aligns correctly.    Looking at the code, the function is:

- grabbing legend widths and axis text widths
- determining the maximum horiz extent of each of these
- redering each graph in a viewport shifted and resized against delta to the above

The code does not account for facet decoration or horizontal spacers.   Also there appears to be a rendering bug with:

 align.plots (Gc, Ga)

where the legend grob is rendered twice? and one is partially truncated  (perhaps this is only in my versions of packages?).  I did:

grid.ls <http://grid.ls>(viewports=T, grob=T)

But could not determine which grobs were associated with facet labels or which would indicate additional horizontal spacing.

Pointers appreciated.

Thanks

Jonathan
--
Systematic Trading LLC

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Indeed, align.plots() is just a bag of tricks I wrote to extract the
total width of ggplot elements and align the plot panels accordingly.
I only considered the most trivial case (no facetting, no fancy
options), mainly because I believe a real solution should be
integrated in the core of ggplot2 (and I think Hadley has been working
on it with a new approach). That said, it might be possible to adapt
align.plots() in the meantime, if you can figure out which sizes are
missing in the calculation.

baptiste

All,

I'm attempting to polish up these cluster plots and wanted a way to refer to each plot within the text of my paper. I plotted the cluster centers easily enough with geom_point(). What I would like to do is to plot the cluster number in black on top of the cluster center to make it visible within the noise. I've been trying without success to use geom_text() to plot these cluster centers using a text symbol so that each cluster will be numbered, 1, 2, 3...etc.

Here is the code that works, without text symbols.

library(ellipse)
library(mclust)
library(ggplot2)

iris_mclust=Mclust(iris[,1:4])

get.ellipses <- function(coords, mclust.fit){
 centers <- mclust.fit$parameters$mean[coords, ]
 vars <- mclust.fit$parameters$variance$sigma[coords, coords, ]
 ldply(1:ncol(centers), function(cluster){
   data.frame(ellipse(vars[,,cluster], centre = centers[, cluster],
     level = 0.5), classification = cluster)
   })
}

iris.el <- get.ellipses(c("Sepal.Length", "Sepal.Width"), iris_mclust)
iris$classification <- iris_mclust$classification

#creates matrix with cluster centers and numbers
cluster_num=cbind(1:nrow(t(iris_mclust$parameters$mean)))
Centers=as.data.frame(cbind(cluster_num, t(iris_mclust$parameters$mean)))
colnames(Centers)=c("clustNum", "Sepal.Length", "Sepal.Width")

ggplot(iris, aes(Sepal.Length, Sepal.Width, colour = factor(classification))) +
 geom_point(aes(shape = classification))+
 geom_path(data = iris.el,

   aes(group = classification, linetype = classification))+

#plots cluster centers
geom_point(data=Centers, aes(x=Sepal.Length, y=Sepal.Width), shape=16, size=3, colour="gray58")

What I tried was adding geom_text() like this:

geom_text(data=Centers, aes(x=Sepal.Length, y=Sepal.Width, label=clustNum))

I get an error - "Error in factor(classification) : object 'classification' not found" - except I don't understand why it needs that factor.

Any help would be appreciated. It seems like this must be simple but I'm not seeing it.

Thanks,

Jens

messages.body_snippet:
Hi:

In place of geom_point() to mark the cluster centers, use

geom_text(data=Centers, aes(x=Sepal.Length, y=Sepal.Width, label = clustNum), size=10, colour="gray58")

Worked for me. If you're going

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the help. Apparently I was under the impression that you didn't need to specify the size and colour if you didn't want to.

While using the large number works I was trying to go for a compound shape, something that would both indicate the exact center and also label the cluster. Using your help this is what I did. Works well and I like the look.

#plots cluster centers with a filled circle and a number within to identify the cluster.
geom_point(data=as.data.frame(Centers), aes(x=Sepal.Length, y=Sepal.Width), shape=16, size=5, colour="gray58") +
geom_text(data=Centers, aes(x=Sepal.Length, y=Sepal.Width, label = clustNum), size=3, colour="black")

Thanks

Jens

messages.body_plain:
Also, yes I agree that after labeling them the legend isn't necessary, nor is color or shape depending on what you are doing. In the plots I'm working on using my research data I've pulled the legend out with a legend=NULL statement in the ggplot() element. The ellipses don't capture all the points though, so having either color or shape is still important to understand where the edges of the cluster are. Using both would be overkill. I'm working in B&W for publication so I cut out color, but given my druthers I think color is easier to quickly interpret.

Jens

Thanks.  I agree that the best solution lies within ggplot itself.    I did a hack where i located that # of y axis titles as in:

getGrob(.g,"axis.text.y.text",grep=TRUE, global=TRUE)

If the # of grobs found > 1, assumed was vertically facetted and added in an estimate of the decoration size (I could not find the grob for it) to be 15pt.   With different fonts or other options, obviously would not work.

Jonathan

messages.subject_clean: insets of non-ggplot2 plots
messages.body_plain:
Scott,

What you are asking to do is very complicated.   First you are trying to mix base graphics (plot) with grid graphics (qplot/ggplot).  Afaik, this cannot be done.  check Paul Murrell's book R graphics.  What you need if you want to do this is either find or write a procedure for visualizing the trees as a grid grob object.  Grobs can then be included through viewports into other grid plots like ggplot.

-Andrew

rowMeans(jenn)

jenn$row.mean <- rowMeans(jenn)

rowMeans(jenn)["r2"]
mean(jenn["r2" ,])

Hi:

Use expand = c(0, 0) in scale_y_continuous()...but you need to be careful, as the following example shows.

d <- structure(list(x = 1:50, y = c(2.22632311995742, 4.20930208812107,
7.69257133173181, 11.4678820426463, 11.3889228872281, 12.964789666021,
14.9892838863793, 16.2579057517061, 20.3697428126379, 19.7722455882214,
23.2962197550043, 25.2820819179160, 24.8895517763587, 29.0665792968226,
30.8196379204549, 33.8473887803161, 35.5028627005978, 39.4445523401192,
39.690849402195, 43.2145274867637, 42.8410118799909, 44.5864427729729,
47.1313483767006, 48.1310295474914, 50.0732779511282, 51.0482220944363,
55.1249583302253, 57.0684756428575, 60.184254246046, 59.8336192477496,
62.6972156781126, 64.6973171194804, 67.7917822920305, 69.5302184880986,
70.6796916043978, 73.548634673699, 74.715812785803, 76.7094404183777,
77.3055555089025, 79.8326412990929, 82.2005648765955, 83.455876938435,
87.266264854227, 88.123819928451, 89.1637923282434, 92.1738365476067,
94.7135682848657, 97.1203279278892, 97.7393565673663, 101.610960107591
)), .Names = c("x", "y"), row.names = c(NA, -50L), class = "data.frame")

ggplot(d, aes(x, y)) + geom_point() +
     scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
     scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0))

ggplot(d, aes(x, y)) + geom_point() +
     scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 50), expand = c(0, 0)) +
     scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 100), expand = c(0, 0))

Look at the points in the lower left and upper right corners of the first plot. As long as you have data that are contained with the plot boundaries you set, there should be no problem, but points close to or on the boundaries will get clipped when you remove the axis padding. Notice that the observation at x = 50 is slightly above 100; the first plot removes the padding but the point is still present, although clipped. In the second plot, since the y-limits are fixed, the point at x = 50 is removed and you get a warning.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.subject: Re: insets of non-ggplot2 plots
messages.subject_clean: insets of non-ggplot2 plots
messages.body_plain:
It sounds like a cool project, but I agree that it sounds difficult.
Is there a reason why the plot needs to be inset before outputting
from R?

I often do things like this by combining two plots in Adobe
Illustrator or some similar vector graphics program. I will admit that
I've not tried this with R plots and don't know much about exporting
as a vector graphics format (.ps, .eps, .svg, etc...) but it looks
like it isn't hard to output plots in these formats. I often spruce up
Excel graphs by exporting as a PDF and opening them in Illustrator,
where it opens as a multilayer vector image. It's amazing how not-
Excel you can make an Excel chart look this way. And when you are done
you can save it at whatever size you like without losing quality.

You could do the same things in an image editor like photoshop using
pixel based images (.jpeg, .bmp, .png, .gif) but with the straight
lines and high contrast of a chart you start running into problems
with visible grainy-ness right away unless you are using extremely
large files. You also don't get the chance to fix individual elements
within the plot using this method, you can only resize and overlay
them.

I realize this is a coding group, and I don't want to take away from
the project. If it can be done in R it would be cool to see how it
gets solved. But, it seems like doing it externally might be alot
quicker unless there is a reason the insets must be done within the
code.

Jens

messages.subject_clean: insets of non-ggplot2 plots
messages.body_plain:
Jens,

I agree that, without easily implemented methods in R already, combining plots etc. would be faster in external programs. However, I am really trying hard to create reproducible research, including displaying data. Plus, if it can be done in R, it is much faster in the long run to run a line of code after fiddling with code in R, than to make graphs in R, export them, manipulate them in another program, then save that as a jpeg, etc.

This does basically what I want using base graphics with gridBase:
##############################
require(ape)
require(gridBase)

# make tree
tree <- rtree(20)

# produce outer ("main") plot
quartz()
plot(1:10,xaxs="i",yaxs="i")
vp <- baseViewports()
pushViewport(vp$inner,vp$figure,vp$plot)

# push viewport that will contain the inset
pushViewport(viewport(x=0.1,y=0.9,width=.5,height=.5,just=c("left","top")))

# define viewport to contain the whole inset figure
par(fig=gridFIG(),new=T) # or gridPLT() # ...or just the plotting are (coordinate system)

# draw frame around selected area, not necessary really
grid.rect(gp=gpar(lwd=3,col="red"))

# plot inset figure
plot(tree, no.margin = TRUE)

But, I want to do so with ggplot2 graphics (which I tried and did not work, trying to plot the tree as inset just created a new graphics window). I tried ggExtra a bit, but nothing pops out as what I need.

Thanks, Scott

On Friday, February 25, 2011 at 10:40 AM, FishGradGuy wrote:

> It sounds like a cool project, but I agree that it sounds difficult.
> Is there a reason why the plot needs to be inset before outputting
> from R?
>
> I often do things like this by combining two plots in Adobe
> Illustrator or some similar vector graphics program. I will admit that
> I've not tried this with R plots and don't know much about exporting
> as a vector graphics format (.ps, .eps, .svg, etc...) but it looks
> like it isn't hard to output plots in these formats. I often spruce up
> Excel graphs by exporting as a PDF and opening them in Illustrator,
> where it opens as a multilayer vector image. It's amazing how not-
> Excel you can make an Excel chart look this way. And when you are done
> you can save it at whatever size you like without losing quality.
>
> You could do the same things in an image editor like photoshop using
> pixel based images (.jpeg, .bmp, .png, .gif) but with the straight
> lines and high contrast of a chart you start running into problems
> with visible grainy-ness right away unless you are using extremely
> large files. You also don't get the chance to fix individual elements
> within the plot using this method, you can only resize and overlay
> them.
>
> I realize this is a coding group, and I don't want to take away from
> the project. If it can be done in R it would be cool to see how it
> gets solved. But, it seems like doing it externally might be alot
> quicker unless there is a reason the insets must be done within the
> code.

> Jens

Hi,

I don't think you can do it currently. You could try this modified
version of GeomPoint and see if it helps,

library(ggplot2)

GeomPoint$draw <- function (., data, scales, coordinates, na.rm = FALSE, ...)
{
    data <- remove_missing(data, na.rm, c("x", "y", "size","width", "shape"),
        name = "geom_point")
    if (empty(data))
        return(zeroGrob())
    with(coordinates$transform(data, scales), ggname(.$my_name(),
        pointsGrob(x, y, size = unit(size, "mm"), pch = shape,
            gp = gpar(col = alpha(colour, alpha), fill = fill,
                fontsize = size * ggplot2:::.pt, lex=width))))
}

GeomPoint$default_aes <-  function (.)
aes(shape = 16, colour = "black", size = 2, fill = NA, alpha = 1,
    width=1)

qplot(1:3, 1:3, shape=1:3, size=I(10))

qplot(1:3, 1:3, shape=1:3, width=I(2), size=I(10))

HTH,

baptiste

If it's only a fixed value, you could simply add the parameter to
GeomPoint$draw_legend,

GeomPoint$draw_legend <- function (., data, ...)
{
    if (!is.null(data$fill) && !all(is.na <http://is.na>(data$fill)) && data$shape ==
        16) {
        data$shape <- 21
    }
    data <- aesdefaults(data, .$default_aes(), list(...))
    with(data, pointsGrob(0.5, 0.5, size = unit(size, "mm"),
        pch = shape, gp = gpar(col = alpha(colour, alpha), fill = alpha(fill,
            alpha), fontsize = size * .pt, lex=size)))
}

However, if you want to map a value to the line width you'll need to
define a new scale,

d <- data.frame(x=1:10,y=rnorm(10),f=rep(letters[1:2], each=5))

qplot(x,y, data=d, shape=f, width=x, size=I(10)) +
  scale_shape_manual(value=c(1,2))

HTH,

baptiste

Hi all-
 I wanted to do something very similar to this, and this thread helped
me get most of the way there. Thanks. Here's my plot:

subj<-c(1:50)
trials1<-floor(runif(50,1,13))
p1<-rbinom(50,trials1,.30)/trials1
trials2<-floor(runif(50,1,13))
p2<-rbinom(50,trials2,.70)/trials2

id<-rep(id,2)
time<-c(rep(1,50),rep(2,50))
trials<-c(trials1,trials2)
p<-c(p1,p2)

w<-data.frame(id,time,trials,p)

ggplot(w, aes(w[,2], w[,4], size=w[,3])) + geom_point() +
	geom_line(aes(group = w[,1]), size=0.25)

However, I want to add one final wrinkle. I'd like to color each
individual line based on the slope of that line. If p1 is the
proportion of successes at time point 1, and p2 is the proportion of
successess at time point 2, then a person with (p1, p2) = (0, 1) would
have, say, a dark blue line. Whereas someone with (p1, p2) = (1, 0)
would have a dark red line. Any line with a slope in between these two
extremes would have a color that falls somewhere in the middle of the
blue:red spectrum. Doable? I used a 'long' dataset to create what I
have. If I used 'wide' dataset, I could add a difference variable,
DIFF=P2-P1, then specify 'Color=DIFF'. But then my 'group = w[,1]'
argument in geom_line() would no longer be valid... Suggestions?

Thanks,
Skyler

At first I thought this would be a one-liner, but it is a little more
complicated than that. Here is one solution:

d <- ddply(w, .(id), function(df) {
    r <- df[df$time==2, "p"] - df[df$time==1, "p"]
    d <- data.frame(id = unique(df$id), diff=r)
    return(d)})
w <- merge(w, d)
ggplot(w, aes(time, p, size=trials)) + geom_point() +
geom_line(size=0.25, aes(group=id, color=diff))

Best,
Ista

4L, 3L, NA, NA, 9L, 19L, 1L, 34L, NA, 53L, 3L, NA, NA, 3L, 6L,
NA, 6L, 2L, 38L, NA, 3L, 2L, 17L, 29L, 36L, NA, 7L, 3L, 3L, 5L,
10L, 2L, 10L, NA, 0L, 1L, 1L, 14L, 18L, 15L, 4L, NA, 41L, 26L,
33L, 10L, NA)), .Names = "x", row.names = c(NA, -142L), class = "data.frame")

ggplot2(visited) + geom_histogram(aes(x=x), binwidth=2, right=FALSE)

I'd like to scale *both* axes to be in percent.  I can do that for the
y-axis like so:

ggplot2(visited) + geom_histogram(aes(x=x, y=..density..), binwidth=2,
right=FALSE) +
    scale_y_continuous(formatter="percent", limits=c(0,.1))

or I can do it for the x-axis like so:

ggplot2(visited) + geom_histogram(aes(x=x/7012), binwidth=2/7012, right=FALSE) +
    scale_x_continuous(formatter="percent", limits=c(0,.02))

(the magic number 7012 is the known-from-experimental-design largest
possible entry in the 'x' vector, which nobody came even remotely
close to)  But if I try to combine the two, logically this *should*
work...

ggplot2(visited) + geom_histogram(aes(x=x/7012, y=..density..),
binwidth=2/7012, right=FALSE) +
    scale_y_continuous(formatter="percent", limits=c(0,.1)) +
    scale_x_continuous(formatter="percent", limits=c(0,.02))

but instead gives me a blank graph.  Removing the limits on the y-axis
restores the graph, but the percentages are ridiculously enormous --
10,000% to 50,000%.  I can only conclude that ..density.. is not
fulfilling its contract to integrate to 1 when the bins are this
narrow.

Any advice?  Is there a better way to do this?

messages.subject: Re: Adding a textbox to a ggplot graph
messages.subject_clean: Adding a textbox to a ggplot graph
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

It's not clear to me where you want this text, but a general advice would be to use grid.text() to place the text anywhere on the device. You could also use grid.table() from gridExtra,

library(ggplot2)
library(gridExtra)

p <- qplot(1:10,1:10, colour=1:10)
labs <- cbind(paste("Q",1:7), paste("answer",1:7))
g <- tableGrob(labs)
grid.arrange(p, g, nrow=1, widths=c(3,1))

HTH,

baptiste

Hi Zack -

I was going to write a more instructive email, but as I started working more on your problem, I realized that I really have no idea what you want.  Generally speaking, if you don't like stat_bin (or it's not calculating what you want), just script the stat yourself and use geom_rect to make the plot.  You can do it in a handful of lines, so it's really easy :

counts <- as.numeric(table(cut(visited$x, breaks = (0:11) * 10)))
df <- data.frame(
  xmin = (0:10) * 10,
  xmax = (1:11) * 10,
  ymin = rep(0, 11),
  ymax = counts
)
ggplot(data = df) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax))

That being said, in most cases the structure of ggplot is there for a reason, especially with something so common as stat_bin, so be careful when you rig your own graphic and strong-arm ggplot into drawing it - you may just be making something that makes no sense or, worse, is misleading.

Hope it helps
david.

OK, I think I see now. I dont' think it can be done well. Esentially
you want to map two variables to the size aesthetic, which will always
be confusing. You can sort of fake it (Brandon  showed a couple of
possibilities) but I think it's best to use another aesthetic. What
about

ggplot(data=aves, aes(x=x, y=y))+geom_point(aes(size=ACE,
color=ACE_SE))+geom_text(aes(x=x+500, label=sitio), size=2, hjust=0)

Best,
Ista

messages.subject: incorrect y-axis positioning in facetted plots
messages.subject_clean: incorrect y-axis positioning in facetted plots
messages.body_plain:
Dear list,

Consider this,

library(ggplot2)

d <- data.frame(x=c(1,1), y=c("a", "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa"),stringsAsFactors=FALSE)

qplot(x,y, data=d) +
  facet_grid(y~.,scales="free")

Both y axis labels and tick marks seem to be centered horizontally; it
is particularly unfortunate for the top tick mark that's inexplicably
far from the plot panel (I don't think this was the case in previous
versions of the package).

Is there an option to fix this and regain the right justification?

Sincerely,

baptiste

subj<-c(1:50)
trials1<-floor(runif(50,1,13))
p1<-rbinom(50,trials1,.30)/trials1
trials2<-floor(runif(50,1,13))
p2<-rbinom(50,trials2,.70)/trials2

id<-rep(subj,2)

time<-c(rep(1,50),rep(2,50))
trials<-c(trials1,trials2)
p<-c(p1,p2)

w<-data.frame(id,time,trials,p)

library(ggplot2)

d <- ddply(w, .(id), function(df) {
   r <- df[df$time==2, "p"] - df[df$time==1, "p"]
   d <- data.frame(id = unique(df$id), diff=r)
   return(d)})
w <- merge(w, d)

ggplot(w2, aes(time, p, size=trials)) + geom_point() +
geom_line(size=0.25, aes(group=id, color=diff))

dim(w)
[1] 100   5

Best,
Ista

messages.subject: plot each layer in its own color

messages.body_plain:
Below are two different syntaxes that explicitly define three layers, each with its own color, and then plot them on top of each other.

But both syntaxes also create a distracting, silly legend.

(1) How can I suppress the legend? But, more important ...

(2) Legend suppression is a workaround. The creation of the legend in the first place suggests that I have not approached the problem correctly. Is there a way to make this plot that does *not* require a workaround?

(3) If there is to be a legend at all, it should say something like "data", "interpolation", "least squares line" and should show in turn a red dot (no line through it), a green line (without dot), and a blue line (without dot). How would one elegantly do that in ggplot2?

# One syntax:

set.seed(7)

DUT<-data.frame(eks=rnorm(9))

DUT$why<-DUT$eks * 0.3 + rnorm(9)/5

pointlayer<-layer(data=DUT, mapping=aes(x=eks, y=why, color="red"), geom="point", geom_params=list(shape=1))

linelayer<-layer(data=DUT, mapping=aes(x=eks, y=why, color="blue"), geom="line")

smoothlayer<- layer(data=DUT, mapping=aes(x=eks, y=why, color="green"), geom="smooth", method="lm", se=FALSE)

ggplot() + pointlayer + linelayer + smoothlayer

# Another syntax:

DUT$pointcolor<- "red"

DUT$linecolor<-"blue"

DUT$smoothcolor<-"green"

pointlayer2<-layer(data=DUT, mapping=aes(x=eks, y=why, color=pointcolor), geom="point", geom_params=list(shape=1))

linelayer2<-layer(data=DUT, mapping=aes(x=eks, y=why, color=linecolor), geom="line")

smoothlayer2<- layer(data=DUT, mapping=aes(x=eks, y=why, color=smoothcolor), geom="smooth", method="lm", se=FALSE)

ggplot() + pointlayer2 + linelayer2 + smoothlayer2

Thanks

messages.body_plain:
If you want to keep using the verbose layer syntax, use

pointlayer<-layer(data=DUT, mapping=aes(x=eks, y=why), color="pink",
geom="point", geom_params=list(shape=1, color="red"))

linelayer<-layer(data=DUT, mapping=aes(x=eks, y=why), geom="line",
geom_parames=list(color="blue"))

smoothlayer<- layer(data=DUT, mapping=aes(x=eks, y=why),
geom="smooth", geom_params=list(color="green"),
stat_params=list(method="lm", se=FALSE))

ggplot() + pointlayer + linelayer + smoothlayer

The main thing you seem to have been tripped up on is the difference
between setting an aesthetic to a fixed value versus mapping it to a
variable. To do the former, set it outside the aes() call (or inside
geom_parames or stat_parames lists as in my example above). To do the
latter, set it inside the aes() call (this will generate a legend
unless you turn it off).

Best,
Ista

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

This appears to get you 99% of the way there, I believe, including the legend:

# The 'shortcut way':
ggplot(data = DUT, aes(x = eks, y = why)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = 'Data'), shape = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(colour = 'Interpolation')) +
  geom_smooth(aes(colour = 'Least squares line'), method = 'lm', se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = 'x', y = 'y', colour = 'Type') +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c('Data' = 'red', 'Interpolation' = 'blue',
                             'Least squares line' = 'green'))

# The layered way:
pointlayer<-layer(data=DUT, mapping=aes(x=eks, y=why, color = 'Data'),
                  geom="point", geom_params=list(shape=1))

linelayer<-layer(data=DUT, mapping=aes(x=eks, y=why, color = 'Interpolation'),
                 geom="line")

smoothlayer<- layer(data=DUT, mapping=aes(x=eks, y=why, color = 'Least squares line'),
                    geom="smooth", stat_params=list(method="lm", se=FALSE))

ggplot() + pointlayer + linelayer + smoothlayer +
  labs(x = 'x', y = 'y') +
  scale_color_manual(name = 'Type',
                     values = c('Data' = 'red', 'Interpolation' = 'blue',
                                'Least squares line' = 'green'))

You'll need a hack to pick and choose among geom types in the legend. The problem is that you use color for both points and lines, so what gets rendered in the legend is (go figure) points and lines. See p. 111 of Hadley's text. In base graphics, there is both an lty and pch argument to legend() - if you want one but not the other, one can be set to NULL in the appropriate location of the vector. There is no such analogue in ggplot2 AFAIK. Hadley could tell you if something is in the works on the development side, or perhaps someone can hack the legend code to add such a feature and post it here. Absent that, the legend glyphs are what they are, and the legend code is behaving as documented.

HTH,
Dennis
